Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
It was at midnight that I received a message from Ryan, desiring that we should meet, for he had something of consequence to say to me; and I was not so little acquainted with such language as to be in any doubt of what it must mean. We met the next day at a shop in the town, where I found him already arrived and engaged with some little trifle of the hand, rather than with his own thoughts. He looked not a little uneasy; and when at length he spoke, it was to say that he was not ready for any serious engagement, and that the fault was in himself and not in me.

I wanted to cry, but I did not; I only bowed my head and made him some short answer of assent, and said that it was all very well. I then walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of iced cream; for in such cases, where the mind cannot be comforted, the appetite must be attended to in its stead.

My companion with whom I shared the room thought that I made more of the matter than it was worth; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me all the same.

faults.quote: engaged with some little trifle of the hand, rather than with his own thoughts
faults.why: The original says he was scrolling on his phone. The rewrite adds a contrast with his thoughts that the writer never made, and 'trifle of the hand' is so vague that the fact is lost.

faults.quote: and said that it was all very well
faults.why: The writer said only 'okay'. 'All very well' carries a note of irony or reluctant acceptance that was not in the original.

faults.quote: for in such cases, where the mind cannot be comforted, the appetite must be attended to in its stead.
faults.why: This is an invented maxim. It is arguably commentary, but it explains the ice cream with a stated reason and a note of mock-philosophy the writer did not give.

faults.quote: he had something of consequence to say to me
faults.why: The writer said only 'we needed to talk'. The rewrite adds something of consequence, and 'desiring that we should meet' changes the text into a request to meet.

faults.quote: I knew right away what that meant.
faults.why: The immediacy and the brevity of the original dread are diluted into a long, cool construction with a double negative, which weakens the sense of knowing at once.

faults.quote: My companion with whom I shared the room
faults.why: This is clumsy and awkward. Austen would say 'my room-mate' or 'the friend who shared my apartments'. The phrase is wordy without being elegant.

faults.quote: a shop in the town
faults.why: The coffee shop is reduced to a vague 'shop', and a coffee shop would be an anachronism. The voice needs a period substitute, and 'downtown' is lost.

faults.quote: I only bowed my head and made him some short answer of assent
faults.why: The writer said she nodded. Bowing the head is more formal, and the long phrase 'short answer of assent' is heavy and slightly comic.

faults.quote: I was not so little acquainted with such language as to be in any doubt of what it must mean.
faults.why: The stacked negatives are overdone, and the Austen irony is aimed at nobody. It reads as pastiche more than as Austen's narrative manner.

faults.quote: but it hurt me all the same.
faults.why: The ending is plain modern idiom ('all the same') and loses the balance that Austen would give the final line. The closing feeling is not tied to any judgement.

faults.quote: I wanted to cry, but I did not
faults.why: The first-person confessional narration is not Austen's manner, but the rewrite does not make up for it with free indirect style or a narrator's irony.

faults.quote: Clauses balanced in one period
faults.why: The cited chapters and paragraphs cannot be verified, and the label 'Speech reported' or 'Feeling shown by conduct' is applied to sentences that merely paraphrase the writer. The citations look like invented references. Paragraph 3 has no notes at all.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “in such cases, where the mind cannot be comforted, the appetite must be attended to in its stead.”
faults.why: The same sentence is annotated twice with different sources, one as 'ironic verdict' and one as 'abstract nouns'. This is redundant, and neither note mentions that the maxim was added to the text.

faults.quote: [structure] Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The notes do not report that the original's 'nodded' became 'bowed my head', that the 'phone' was obscured, or that 'okay' changed register, so the changes are not reported.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the main events in order but blurs the phone, alters 'okay' and the nod, and adds an invented maxim. The diction is stiff and sometimes awkward ('My companion with whom I shared the room'), and the notes cite doubtful sources while leaving the real changes unreported.

yours:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
My dear Father and Mother, Camp, upon the whole, is tolerably well, though I cannot pretend that my expectations have been answered; and I find that the society, as is generally the case in such places, has more of form than of comfort in it. The food is not such as I could wish, and my companion in the bedchamber lies awake half the night, or sleeps so loud that nobody else can; but these are evils which I am learning to bear with composure. Yesterday we went upon the water, and whether from want of skill or of attention I know not, I had the misfortune to overturn the boat, and was taken up in a state which afforded great entertainment to the whole party; I was not a little mortified by it.

There is, however, a young lady of the name of Kayla whose acquaintance has been a real comfort to me, and I think her by far the pleasantest girl of all the party. She is from the country, and what is still more to her credit in my eyes, she knows a great deal of horses; we sit together by the lake after dinner, and talk of everything that interests us both, so that the time passes with me better than I could have hoped. I believe she likes me, though I cannot be quite sure of it, and I should be sorry to flatter myself where there was no foundation.

I wish you would be so good as to send me some refreshments, for the food here does not quite answer to my appetite; and my little machine for writing, which I entirely forgot, I beg you would send likewise, for I am much in want of it. The people who have the care of us are rather strict, but in the main they behave with great propriety, and I have no very great fault to find with them.

Your affectionate son, Jake.

P.S. I beg you will not let Max use my room while I am away.

faults.quote: She is from the country
faults.why: The original says she is from Ohio. The specific place is replaced with a vague 'country', so a fact is lost. 'The country' also means something different from a state.

faults.quote: or sleeps so loud that nobody else can
faults.why: The bunkmate 'snores like crazy'. The rewrite turns this into insomnia plus loud sleep, which is garbled and adds an invented detail ('lies awake half the night').

faults.quote: and was taken up in a state which afforded great entertainment
faults.why: Adds a rescue ('taken up'). The original only says everybody laughed. The laughter is also blurred into 'entertainment'.

faults.quote: for the food here does not quite answer to my appetite
faults.why: This repeats the food complaint as a reason for the snacks. The original gives no reason and the food was 'gross', so the force is weakened. It is also redundant.

faults.quote: whether from want of skill or of attention I know not
faults.why: Adds a speculation about the cause of the capsizing that the writer never made.

faults.quote: while I am away
faults.why: Small addition to the P.S. that is not in the original.

faults.quote: I think her by far the pleasantest girl of all the party
faults.why: Inflates 'really cool' into a comparative superlative over all the girls. This is a new claim.

faults.quote: my little machine for writing
faults.why: A circumlocution for the phone charger that actually names a typewriter or pen. It is a riddle and the wrong object. A charger is not a writing machine, so the sense is lost.

faults.quote: Camp, upon the whole, is tolerably well, though I cannot pretend that my expectations have been answered
faults.why: Adds disappointed expectations the writer never expressed. 'Okay I guess' is not the same as unmet expectations. The 'society... more of form than of comfort' clause is also invented.

faults.quote: my little machine for writing, which I entirely forgot, I beg you would send likewise
faults.why: The phone charger is turned into something unrelated and the mending is not reported. The rewrite also leaves out that the charger is for a phone. The clause is clumsy as well.

faults.quote: My dear Father and Mother, Camp, upon the whole,
faults.why: The letter opening runs straight into the body with no line break. The result reads as a pastiche and the rewrite also lacks Austen's ironic play. It has mostly stock phrases.

faults.quote: cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 13, ¶ 62
faults.why: The label 'Feeling shown by conduct' does not fit the snoring line, which is a complaint rather than feeling shown by action. The citations also look unverifiable and are used for generic moves.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “I was taken up in a state which afforded great entertainment to the whole party; I was not a little mortified by it.”
faults.why: This duplicates the litotes note by quoting the same sentence. The notes also say nothing of the changes made to the facts (Ohio, charger, added expectations) and give no 'sense' mending report.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2 (renders the writer’s ¶3):
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 2, 4 and 5 carry no notes, though they contain significant changes such as 'the country' and the 'machine for writing'. The writer is not told about these.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a pleasant Austenian surface, but it garbles or changes several facts: Ohio becomes 'the country', the snoring becomes insomnia, the phone charger becomes a 'machine for writing', and invented expectations and a rescue are added. The notes do not flag any of these and are thin and partly mislabeled.

The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
The office was of a size and fashion to which nothing in my former experience had the least resemblance; the furniture, and every article within it, was in all the profusion and elegance of modern taste, and I could not look upon it without suspecting that every person in it must be a person of consequence. The company wore, every one of them, the rough common dress of the town, and carried about their cups of coffee with an air of perfect ease; and I, in my suit, felt myself altogether out of place among them, like a walking testimony to my own want of consequence.

The manager was a woman named Priya, and her manners were all that could be wished in point of friendliness; yet there was in her eye and address something rather too earnest, which made her, to a stranger, not a little formidable. She asked me about my powers and my weaknesses—for by neither of those names, I am convinced, would she have called them; and I, with a composure I was very far from feeling, replied that my great fault was a too anxious desire of doing every thing perfectly; an answer so common as to be scarce worth the giving, and which I had the mortification of seeing was not lost upon her. She smiled, however, and that smile, so much at variance with my own notion of what I deserved, sunk me a very little lower.

As soon as the interview was over, I called upon my sister, and related to her, with all the eagerness of a mind in suspense, the particulars of the hour I had passed. She heard me to the end, and then declared herself of opinion that I had most probably done excellently well; and it is her being right that I trust for above every thing, because I am in the greatest need of this situation; for the rent is due next week, and I have, at this moment, scarce five pounds in the world.

faults.quote: that smile, so much at variance with my own notion of what I deserved, sunk me a very little lower
faults.why: The writer's 'She smiled anyway' is a mild relief. The rewrite makes the smile deflate the narrator, which reverses the feeling.

faults.quote: which I had the mortification of seeing was not lost upon her
faults.why: This adds an incident: the interviewer visibly noticing the narrator's weak answer. The writer only said the answer was lame.

faults.quote: I could not look upon it without suspecting that every person in it must be a person of consequence
faults.why: This adds a new thought, that the staff are important people. It is more than commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: like a walking testimony to my own want of consequence
faults.why: This adds self-deprecation and intensifies the writer's mild 'out of place'. It also repeats 'consequence' from the previous sentence.

faults.quote: scarce five pounds in the world
faults.why: The writer said only 'basically broke'. The specific sum is invented.

faults.quote: it is her being right that I trust for above every thing
faults.why: 'I hope she's right' becomes strong trust and dependence. The degree of feeling shifts, and the sentence is clumsy.

faults.quote: carried about their cups of coffee with an air of perfect ease
faults.why: 'Fancy' coffee is lost, and 'hoodies' becomes the vague 'rough common dress of the town'. Both details are blurred.

faults.quote: for by neither of those names, I am convinced, would she have called them
faults.why: This is an unexplained aside that contradicts the plain fact that she asked about strengths and weaknesses. It introduces confusion into a clear draft, and the notes do not report it.

faults.quote: I called upon my sister
faults.why: In Austen's idiom 'called upon' means a visit in person, not a telephone call. It is a misused sense.

faults.quote: I called upon my sister, and related to her, with all the eagerness of a mind in suspense, the particulars of the hour I had passed
faults.why: This is padding, and it adds an eager full retelling the writer never gave.

faults.quote: my powers and my weaknesses
faults.why: 'Powers' is an awkward substitute for 'strengths', and the following dash sentence makes it more confusing.

faults.quote: and it is her being right that I trust for above every thing, because I am in the greatest need of this situation; for the rent is due next week
faults.why: The sentence is a clumsy pile of 'because' and 'for' clauses with a shifting tense. It is not Austen's controlled periodic balance.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “and it is her being right that I trust for above every thing
faults.why: The label does not fit the passage, which is earnest need rather than irony. The cited source, Lady Susan 'ch. 17 ¶ 4', is doubtful for an epistolary work.

faults.quote: Feeling shown by conduct: “She smiled, however, and that smile
faults.why: The quoted passage is narratorial self-judgement, not feeling shown by conduct. The specific chapter and paragraph citations look unreliable.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns
faults.why: The notes never mention the added content, the invented figure, or the 'powers' aside. They report no sense mendings, although the rewrite changed the text in these places.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has some Austenian cadence and diction, but it adds incidents and feelings, reverses the smile's effect, invents a sum of money, and introduces a confusing 'powers' aside. The notes mislabel moves and give doubtful pinpoint citations without admitting the changes.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family removed into the house next door at the close of the last week, with a great cart of furniture and two little children. The father, it was soon agreed, seemed a very good sort of man; and it was not long before it appeared that he was in the law, was single, or, to speak more precisely, had been parted from his wife.

My mother, whose curiosity was not to be resisted by any distance, lost not a moment in sending over a plate of biscuits, and in so doing opened an acquaintance which was to answer every purpose of her heart. Her enquiries were soon directed to every particular of their situation; where they came from, what they did for their living, and whether they went to church, were questions which followed one another with a zeal that did her great credit.

My mother's countenance, on hearing it, wore an expression which I perfectly understood; for she had been labouring for years to see me settled, and here was a man whom her imagination could hardly fail to convert into a husband.

notes.text: The first paragraph gives the new family a mother, but the third says the father is single and divorced: a man whose wife shares his house is not single. The passage contradicts itself. I removed the mother, so that the father, single and parted from his wife, agrees with everything said of the household. This is the least change, and it lets the mother's matchmaking designs fall naturally on him.

faults.quote: The father, it was soon agreed, seemed a very good sort of man; and it was not long before it appeared
faults.why: The standoffish mother is deleted outright, so the writer's fact 'The mom is kind of standoffish' is lost. The two characterisations of the household are reduced to one.

faults.quote: I removed the mother, so that the father, single and parted from his wife, agrees
faults.why: The contradiction is caught and reported, but the mending deletes a fact instead of reassigning it. The woman could have been a sister, housekeeper or other relation who stays standoffish. Deleting her leaves the writer's observation unrepresented.

faults.quote: The father, it was soon agreed, seemed a very good sort of man; and it was not long before it appeared that he was in the law
faults.why: The order is changed: the lawyer and divorce revelation now comes before the mother's baking and enquiries, but the writer reveals it afterwards. 'It was soon agreed' also invents a consensus among neighbours.

faults.quote: My mother's countenance, on hearing it, wore an expression
faults.why: 'it' has no antecedent, because the revelation was moved to paragraph 1. The reader cannot tell what she heard, and the cause-and-effect of the writer's 'Well, divorced. My mom got this look' is blurred.

faults.quote: in so doing opened an acquaintance which was to answer every purpose of her heart
faults.why: This adds an outcome not in the original, namely that the acquaintance will serve her purposes. The baking is also reduced to 'sending over a plate', so the baking itself is dropped.

faults.quote: whose curiosity was not to be resisted by any distance
faults.why: This is an odd, near-meaningless phrase. The neighbour is next door, so distance is irrelevant, and the litotes does not land.

faults.quote: with a great cart of furniture
faults.why: 'Huge truck' becomes a cart, and 'of furniture' is added. This is a period substitution, but it changes the detail slightly.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “The father, it was soon agreed, seemed a very good sort of man”
faults.why: The sentence contains no abstract nouns, so the label does not describe the move. The cited source is doubtful for it.

faults.quote: Clauses balanced in one period: “A new family removed into the house next door at the close of the last week, with a great cart of furniture and two little children.”
faults.why: The sentence is a plain loose sentence with no balanced clauses, so the move is mislabelled.

faults.quote: Speech reported: “what they did for their living, and whether they went to church, were questions which followed one another”
faults.why: This is narrated enquiry, not reported speech, so the label is loose.

faults.quote: while changing no fact of the passage
faults.why: This is false, because the mother is removed and her standoffishness is lost. The echo-of-Pride-and-Prejudice note is also put under 'sense' though it is not a fault mending.

faults.quote: did her great credit
faults.why: The ironic praise is Austenian, but much of the rest is generic period diction. There is little of Austen's free indirect style or her sharp, epigrammatic framing.

judge.verdict: The prose is passably period-flavoured and the mother's matchmaking irony is well caught. The mend for the contradiction deletes the standoffish mother instead of reassigning her, the order of revelation is shuffled so 'on hearing it' dangles, and several move labels in the notes are inaccurate.

The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:

faults.quote: Let every one, therefore, have his own part

The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
The office was a place of such extent and so very modern in its fittings that a stranger entering it felt his own plain clothing to be a kind of trespass; for everyone about him was clad in loose garments of the sort worn by persons at ease in the morning, and drank a coffee that had been prepared with more care than is commonly given to that innocent drink. We are all of us aware how such surroundings act upon a mind already doubtful of its claims; and I, in my suit, which had seemed very well at home, felt myself to be quite out of the place, as if the very chairs and tables knew that I had brought with me neither loose garment nor costly cup to offer them.

The manager was a woman named Priya, and her manner at first was friendly, so that I gathered courage; but there was in her a certain intensity, not disagreeable, yet such as made a plain answer seem a thing to be weighed and reweighed before it was spoken. She asked me then what I counted among my powers, and what my weaknesses were—an inquiry before which few of us can stand entirely at ease, since whatever is said of one's own deserving carries with it the suspicion of vanity, and whatever is owned of one's failing the suspicion of a deeper failing still hidden. I answered that I was one of those persons who can never leave a thing half done; which, as a reply, was weaker than I had meant it to be, and I knew it as soon as it was spoken. She smiled nevertheless, with the look of one who had heard such answers before, and was not the less content with them for that.

When the interview was over I called my sister, and told her the whole as well as I could; and she said that I had probably succeeded in getting the job—a prophecy in which I could read no more than that I had not openly disgraced myself. I hope she is right, for the truth must be owned that I am in real need of this job, the rent being due within the week and my purse very nearly empty.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family came to the house next door within the last week, with a great wagon of their goods and two little children; and we are all of us, I suppose, a little stirred at seeing an unfamiliar household settle so near, and cannot help drawing up our private history of it in advance. The father seemed a good-natured sort of man; his sister, who kept the house, was of a colder, less open temper, as if she did not mean to be questioned.

My mother, for her part, carried them biscuits almost at once, for she was never easy till she had learned where a new neighbor came from, how he got his bread, and whether he went to any place of worship: a woman whose kindness and curiosity were so mixed in her that she could not have told them apart, and whose mind was already turning the newcomer into a husband for me.

It came out, in the course of a little talk, that the father was a lawyer, and that he was single—or rather, to speak accurately, divorced; and at this last word my mother's face took a look which I knew as well as I knew her voice, and which told me, without a syllable, what was working within. For she has been trying these many years to marry me to some good woman, and here was a man set free again; and it is a hard thing to stop a mother who has once got such a purpose fairly before her—though, to be sure, it is no very dreadful purpose, and a mother may be forgiven a little scheming of that sort.

The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

He said the party was lame and the people were boring. Emma rolled her eyes. I thought he was rude. But later I saw him helping clean up when everyone else left. Maybe I was wrong about him.
rewrite:
The party was at Jessica's house, and her parents, being from home on affairs of their own, had left it for this one evening to the young people of the school, who had the run of every room; and the music, which was of a sort that no mother present would have willingly allowed, was raised to a volume that filled the whole house, and set the very air beating against one's ears.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, neither of us knowing many of the company; and we are all of us a little chilled where the faces are strange, since the gaiety that was meant to draw us together only makes us feel how little we belong to it—as if a party at which one knows nobody were among the most instructive of schools. While we stood in that quiet corner, a tall young man came over to us and began to talk, with an ease that showed him at home wherever he found himself; and his name was Chris. He had in his manner a kind of arrogant freedom, which yet did not shut out a certain power of making one laugh, so that while I was half disposed to resent him, I could not wholly refuse to be amused.

Before long he said that the party was a dull affair and the people in it tedious; and I felt, without being able to say why, a small vexation at the words, as something warm in me had suddenly met a cold current—the way the easy warmth of a room is checked by one careless breath. Emma rolled her eyes at this, and I thought him rude—as indeed he was; for there is a common duty of courtesy even among the young, and the guests of a house ought not to speak ill of the feast they are sharing. But afterwards, when the rest were gone, I saw him helping to clear away the glasses, with a willingness that no one had asked of him; and I began to think that I had perhaps judged him too hastily, since we so often judge a man wrongly by the first hour of his company.

faults.quote: had left it for this one evening to the young people of the school, who had the run of every room
faults.why: The writer only said the parents were out of town. The rewrite adds that the parents deliberately left the house to the young people, and that the guests had the run of every room.

faults.quote: which was of a sort that no mother present would have willingly allowed
faults.why: This is an invented judgment about mothers and the music. The writer only said it was super loud.

faults.quote: as if a party at which one knows nobody were among the most instructive of schools
faults.why: The writer never said the party was instructive, and this is an invented moral. The ironic aside is not tied to anything in the draft and muddles the plain statement that they didn't know many people.

faults.quote: I felt, without being able to say why, a small vexation at the words, as something warm in me had suddenly met a cold current
faults.why: The writer only said Emma rolled her eyes and the narrator thought him rude. The rewrite invents a vexation and an inner warmth that the narrator never mentions.

faults.quote: and the guests of a house ought not to speak ill of the feast they are sharing
faults.why: This adds a moral lecture that goes beyond the writer's 'I thought he was rude'. It turns the narrator's impression into a general rule.

faults.quote: as indeed he was
faults.why: The narrator only thought him rude, and the draft ends in doubt ("Maybe I was wrong"). This asserts that he really was rude, which makes the narrator's earlier opinion firmer than the writer's.

faults.quote: with a willingness that no one had asked of him
faults.why: This is invented. The writer did not say nobody asked him to help, and 'glasses' is also an invented detail.

faults.quote: since we so often judge a man wrongly by the first hour of his company
faults.why: This turns the writer's tentative 'Maybe I was wrong about him' into a general maxim and more settled certainty. It also loses the tentativeness.

faults.quote: when the rest were gone, I saw him helping to clear away
faults.why: The writer said he helped 'when everyone else left', so the sense is that the others had gone while he stayed. This is roughly kept, but 'afterwards' loses the contrast that he stayed after everyone else left.

faults.quote: being from home on affairs of their own
faults.why: This is awkward and odd. It adds an invented reason (affairs of their own) and does not read idiomatically.

faults.quote: and his name was Chris
faults.why: This is flat and tacked on with a semicolon. 'Chris' is jarring in a Victorian register, and the clause sits oddly after the long sentence about his ease.

faults.quote: and we are all of us a little chilled where the faces are strange
faults.why: The sudden tense shift into a general present, and the 'as if' clause that follows, break the sentence and read as a pasted maxim.

faults.quote: set the very air beating against one's ears
faults.why: This is a generic Victorian-flavored flourish. Eliot's actual manner is more analytic and ironic, with fewer decorative images.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 15, ¶ 3
faults.why: The notes give precise chapter and paragraph citations that cannot be verified and look fabricated. Many of the cited passages do not seem to match the moves (for instance Romola for 'inner life' and a room-warmth analogy).

faults.quote: [move] The narrator’s “we”
faults.why: The notes do not report that new content was added (the mothers, the instructive school, the moral of courtesy, the maxim about judging). They label additions as 'moves' without admitting that they change the meaning.

faults.quote: Emma rolled her eyes at this, and I thought him rude—as indeed he was
faults.why: The rewrite introduces a conflict between the narrator's closing doubt and this firm verdict, a slight inconsistency that the notes do not report.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a Victorian surface, but it adds a lot of invented material (mothers, instruction, warm and cold currents, moral maxims) and firms up the narrator's opinions beyond what the writer said. The notes give suspiciously exact citations and do not disclose the additions.

I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
I needed milk; and having been made sensible, as we all of us are at such moments, that the want would not satisfy itself, I took my keys and drove to the store. It was crowded beyond what the place, in any reasonable expectation, could be thought to hold. A man in a coarse woollen garment drawn over his head stood across the whole aisle, absorbed in talk with some unseen hearer through the instrument he held to his ear—a useful reminder, did we but read it so, that the world is not arranged for our convenience.

I did not wish to be rude, for there is no small unkindness in thrusting oneself upon a stranger's notice; so I begged his pardon in a low voice, as gently as the thing could be said. He took not the least heed, as though my words had dropped into water and left no ripple. It was only after some further minutes that he moved aside with the slow unwillingness of one disturbed in a serious matter, and I was then able to reach the milk. And there, at the desk where goods are paid for, I saw her whom I had once known and loved; and a dread seized me that had in it more of blind fright than of reason.

"Hey," she said, looking up with a steady cheerfulness. "Long time no see. You look well."

"Thanks," I answered; "and you also." I paid and left as fast as I could, carrying my small burden out into the air as one who has long been held in a crowded room. It was, to speak plainly, the most awkward ten minutes of my week; and I went away wondering at the strange power which a chance meeting has to disorder the whole current of one's thoughts.

faults.why: This is a heavy and faintly mock-heroic opening for a trivial need. The 'we' generalization is imposed, and the voice is closer to pastiche than to Eliot's grounded irony.

faults.why: The label does not match the quoted text, which is a periphrasis for 'hoodie' and no scientific or natural analogy. The cited source is dubious.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a period flavor, but it adds invented feelings, durations and moralizing, and it leaves modern slang in the dialogue. The notes mislabel moves, quote text that differs from the rewrite, and cite questionable sources, so it teaches little reliably.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

To the company of our undertaking, greeting:

There is small change to tell of, and you shall have it in few words: the work we had set for Tuesday is now put over to Thursday. The lawyers have not yet set their hand to the page of prices, and I will not have it go forth from us without their mark upon it; which is but a man's way of confessing that he would sooner put off a thing than send it out unfinished and hope for the best.

Let each of you, I entreat, bring his part of the leaves of the deck to its ending by Wednesday at noon. And should any of you find himself stayed, and unable to go forward, speak it to me today, and not wait for the morrow, when the time for mending will be gone from us.

With thanks, Sam

faults.why: Invented clause adding a new self-characterising confession and sentiment not in the original. It goes beyond commenting on what is there and reads as a new claim about the writer's motives.

faults.quote: the work we had set for Tuesday
faults.why: The writer said the launch moves. Rendering it as 'the work' blurs a key fact (the launch) and loses its specificity.

faults.quote: when the time for mending will be gone from us
faults.why: Adds a rationale (no time left to fix things) that the original lacks. The writer only said to tell today, not tomorrow, and the added consequence changes the urgency.

faults.quote: I will not have it go forth from us without their mark upon it
faults.why: The writer's mild 'I don't want us shipping without it' becomes a stern 'I will not have it'. The degree of feeling is raised.

faults.quote: To the company of our undertaking, greeting:
faults.why: An odd, archaic opening that reads like a letter from a guild, not Eliot. 'Company of our undertaking' is a riddle-like phrase.

faults.quote: There is small change to tell of
faults.why: 'Small change' suggests coins or a trivial matter, and it undersells a launch delay. It is unclear and slightly comic. The 'few words' clause is also awkward.

faults.quote: bring his part of the leaves of the deck to its ending
faults.why: 'Leaves of the deck' is clumsy and the stacked 'of' phrases garble the meaning. 'Deck' stays modern in an archaic frame.

faults.quote: I entreat
faults.why: Too biblical or pleading for Eliot's urbane narrator, and out of proportion to a routine request. The whole piece is archaic pastiche (shall, entreat, greeting) rather than Eliot's reflective, ironic, sympathetic narration.

faults.quote: Litotes: “There is small change to tell of, and you shall have it in few words”
faults.why: This is not litotes, which is understatement by negating the contrary. The label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Moral nouns: “and I will not have it go forth from us without their mark upon it”
faults.why: The quoted sentence contains no moral nouns, so the label is wrong. The passage is also not the one that would carry the move.

faults.quote: The narrator’s “we”: “and not wait for the morrow, when the time for mending will be gone from us”
faults.why: There is no narratorial 'we' here, only 'from us'. The note mislabels the move, and the notes ignore the substantial added clause about the man's confession.

faults.why: The notes list phantom paragraphs (1 and 4) and number the paragraphs inconsistently with the rewrite, which has only three. None of the notes flags the additions, so the writer is not told what was added.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the email shape and both requests, but it adds an invented 'confession' clause and a rationale about time, heightens the tone, and uses stilted archaic phrasing ('company of our undertaking', 'leaves of the deck'). The notes mislabel several moves and report none of the additions.

Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.

The Saturday, as it happened, was one of those days in which small labours find their reward in being finished: I cleaned the gutters, I made good the sink which had grown porous, and I called upon my grandmother, who kept me an hour and more with the history of her neighbour's cat.

By the evening I was thoroughly spent; and yet there was mixed with my fatigue a satisfaction in having done my duty by the day, which I could call by no humbler name than pride. We are all of us apt enough to entertain such pride over work that is done and done alone, and I should hardly have confessed it to a friend.

faults.why: The original said the sink was leaky and that the writer fixed it. 'Porous' changes the nature of the fault, since a leaky sink is not a porous one, and 'made good' is vaguer than 'fixed'.

faults.quote: which I could call by no humbler name than pride
faults.why: The original has 'weirdly proud', a light, self-amused feeling. Here the pride is made weighty and moralised ('duty by the day'), which shifts its degree and its tone.

faults.why: This adds claims the writer never made: that the work was done alone, and that the writer would not confess the pride to a friend. The 'we' commentary is allowed, but the confession is a new fact about the writer's behaviour.

faults.quote: in which small labours find their reward in being finished
faults.why: This is an added generalisation. It is mild commentary, but it pre-empts the pride that the writer reaches only in the evening.

faults.quote: kept me an hour and more
faults.why: The original says she talked for an hour. 'An hour and more' exaggerates slightly. 'Kept me' also makes the writer's captivity explicit, which the original does not say.

faults.quote: I called upon my grandmother
faults.why: 'Called upon' means a visit in person, whereas the original is a telephone call. The idiom gives the wrong sense and makes it seem the writer went to her house.

faults.quote: I cleaned the gutters, I made good the sink
faults.why: The anaphoric 'I... I...' is choppy for Eliot's periodic, subordinated syntax. The first paragraph is a plain list with little of her ironic narratorial stance.

faults.quote: cites Middlemarch, ch. 37, ¶ 65
faults.why: Three of the four notes mark the same sentence as separate moves, which is padding. The citations are precise-looking but not clearly apt, and they pile onto one sentence.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps all three tasks and the pride. But 'called upon' misstates a phone call, 'porous' alters the sink's fault, and an invented reluctance to confess the pride is added. The voice is only partly Eliot, and the notes over-cite one sentence while leaving paragraph 1 unannotated.

faults.why: Adds a moral generalisation that goes beyond commentary on the facts and reinterprets the writer's deadpan irony as a sermon on temper. It is arguably more than commentary.

faults.quote: I have been to Paris only once
faults.why: The mending asserts it was once only; the writer said 'the last time', which implies more than one visit. This introduces a new fact and makes it less faithful. The mend also loses the writer's possible joke.

faults.quote: and on the second day my brother lost his passport
faults.why: The plain, brisk statement is merged into one long sentence, losing the writer's two-beat comic timing; Eliot's irony is present but the passage is overstuffed with semicolons and clauses, giving a pastiche feel.

faults.quote: he keeps to this day to saying that it was the pleasantest holiday
faults.why: 'keeps to … to saying' is clumsy and awkward, a doubled 'to'.

faults.quote: in that manner of waiting which makes a foreign city seem to us only a weary room in which we sit
faults.why: Muddled image: a city seeming a room in which we sit is strained, and 'that manner of waiting' is vague.

faults.quote: Analogy from science and nature: “in that manner of waiting which makes a foreign city seem to us only a weary room in which we sit”
faults.why: Mislabelled: the phrase is not an analogy from science or nature, and so the move name does not fit the change.

faults.quote: Moral nouns: “so little do our pleasures depend on the weather or the luck of the hour”
faults.why: The phrase does not clearly use moral nouns; the same quote is also double-counted under another move, and the citations (specific chapters and paragraphs) look unreliable or unverifiable.

faults.quote: This removes the contradiction while keeping every other detail intact.
faults.why: Claim is false: the rewrite added several details (strangers, papers, weariness, vividness of memory, moral) and the notes do not report these additions. The notes also do not mention that the 'last time' implies earlier visits, which the mend contradicts.

faults.quote: I have been to Paris only once
faults.why: The mend is workable, but it conflicts with 'the last time I was there', which implies multiple visits; a better mend would keep the plural or join the two statements.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches and reports the contradiction, but it invents extra content (vivid memory, strangers, weary waiting, a moral about temper), and the 'only once' mend clashes with 'the last time'. The voice is partial, a few phrases are clumsy, and the notes mislabel moves and falsely claim every detail was kept intact.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana set off our dinner, I was not, I think, in any distress at all. Indeed I was relieved; relieved as one is when a burden that has been carried in silence is at last lifted and laid down. I had been dreading the evening all the week long, and I am not proud of that, for we are all of us apt to shrink from what we have undertaken, and to call our shrinking by gentler names.

So I told her it was quite well, and that we should find another time for it. Only I do not think we ever shall.

faults.quote: When Dana set off our dinner
faults.why: "Set off" does not mean cancel. It reads as a malapropism, since "set off" suggests departing or igniting. "Put off" would mean postponing, which is also not cancelling.

faults.quote: for we are all of us apt to shrink from what we have undertaken, and to call our shrinking by gentler names.
faults.why: This adds a new claim and a generalization about self-deception that the writer did not make. It goes beyond voice commentary and imputes euphemism to the writer. The writer's "I'm not proud of that" is plain.

faults.quote: relieved as one is when a burden that has been carried in silence is at last lifted and laid down.
faults.why: The simile adds the idea of a burden carried in silence, which the writer never said. It also over-intensifies the relief.

faults.quote: I was not, I think, in any distress at all.
faults.why: The writer says "wasn't upset at all" flatly. The hedge "I think" softens the certainty, and "distress" is heavier than "upset".

faults.quote: Only I do not think we ever shall.
faults.why: "Ever" is slightly stronger than the writer's "I don't think we will". "Only" adds a rueful contrast. "Quite well" for "fine" is also a slight shift.

faults.quote: all the week long
faults.why: This is a folksy phrase and not characteristic of Eliot's narrative register. The overall effect is generic Victorian pastiche rather than Eliot's analytic, ironic, sympathetic narration. There is also no real Eliot-style syntactic subordination.

faults.quote: Analogy from science and nature: “relieved as one is when a burden that has been carried in silence is at last lifted and laid down.”
faults.why: The label is wrong. A burden lifted is neither science nor nature. The citation to Romola looks arbitrary.

faults.quote: The qualified period: “When Dana set off our dinner, I was not, I think, in any distress at all.” — cites The Mill on the Floss, ch. 17, ¶ 46
faults.why: The same sentence is cited twice for two different moves, with two different sources (ch. 17 and ch. 16). The move names are vague and the paragraph citations look unverifiable. Nothing flags the added generalization as an addition. Paragraph 2 gets no notes even though it was changed ("So", "Only").

faults.quote: The inner life, from inside: “I had been dreading the evening all the week long, and I am not proud of that.”
faults.why: This is a near-verbatim restatement of the writer's own sentence, so it names no real change. The note does not teach anything.

judge.verdict: The relief, dread and doubt all point the right way, but "set off" misrenders "cancelled", and the added moralizing and burden simile go beyond the original. The voice is a Victorian costume more than Eliot, and the notes are mislabeled and padded with dubious citations.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Once upon a time Ryan sent me word at midnight that we must have some talk together. I knew at once what that meant.

The next day we met at a house in the town where they sell coffee, and he was there before me, looking at his little screen and moving his thumb across it. He looked nervous, and when I had sat down he said he was not ready for anything serious, and that it was not me, but him.

I wanted to cry, but I did not; I only nodded and said, All right. Then I walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of it—which, if it was little comfort, was comfort of a kind.

My friend who shares my room with me thought I made too much of it, and maybe I did; but it hurt me all the same.

faults.quote: and ate a whole pint of it—which, if it was little comfort, was comfort of a kind.
faults.why: "of it" has no antecedent, since ice cream is never named; the rain is the nearest noun, so it reads as eating a pint of rain. The writer's ice cream is lost.

faults.quote: which, if it was little comfort, was comfort of a kind
faults.why: Adds a new evaluative claim, that the ice cream gave some comfort. The writer never says this. It is more than the voice's commentary on what is there and softens the hurt.

faults.quote: and he was there before me, looking at his little screen and moving his thumb across it
faults.why: "Scrolling on his phone" is turned into a vague periphrasis. "Moving his thumb" is added detail, and "little screen" is a coy circumlocution.

faults.quote: and when I had sat down he said
faults.why: Adds the narrator sitting down, an event not in the original. It also makes the nervous look and the statement run together.

faults.quote: My friend who shares my room with me
faults.why: "Roommate" becomes a clumsy periphrasis, and "friend" adds a relationship the writer did not state.

faults.quote: a house in the town where they sell coffee
faults.why: Reads as a riddle rather than fairy-book diction. It also drops "downtown" and the coffee shop as a shop.

faults.quote: sent me word at midnight that we must have some talk together
faults.why: Awkward. "Texted" and "We needed to talk" lose the natural idiom, and "some talk together" is not idiomatic even for archaic prose.

faults.quote: I wanted to cry, but I did not; I only nodded and said, All right.
faults.why: Fairy-book prose rarely uses this semicolon-and-unquoted-speech pattern, and the whole piece stays in first-person modern emotional reportage. The voice is mostly archaic word swaps, not real Lang cadence.

faults.quote: and ate a whole measure of it, which, if it was little comfort, was comfort of a kind
faults.why: The quoted note text does not match the rewrite, which says "pint", not "measure", and has a dash, not "which" directly. The note misreports the text.

faults.quote: Antithesis: “I wanted to cry, but I did not.” — cites The Red Fairy Book, “Soria Moria Castle”, ¶ 25
faults.why: The citations are paragraph-specific and seem implausible for such generic moves. "And so, and then" is given for a sentence with neither, and the notes never flag the vague "of it" or the added comfort claim.

faults.quote: thought I made too much of it, and maybe I did; but it hurt me all the same.
faults.why: "Overreacting" is rendered acceptably, but "it still hurt" becomes "all the same", which shifts the nuance slightly. Minor.

judge.verdict: The rewrite reads as stiff archaic word-swapping with a dangling "of it" that turns ice cream into rain, plus an invented comfort claim. The notes misquote the text and cite sources dubiously, so it teaches little.

Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is all right, I suppose, but the food is very bad, and the friend who sleeps in my room snores very loudly. Yesterday we went out in the canoes, and my canoe turned over, and everybody laughed at me, and I was greatly ashamed; and that is what comes of going on the water.

But there is a girl here named Kayla, and she is very pleasant; she comes from Ohio, and she knows a great deal about horses. We sit by the lake after dinner and talk about many things, and I think she likes me, but I am not sure.

Will you send me some more good things to eat, and also a charger for the instrument by which I speak with you, which I forgot altogether? The counsellors here are somewhat strict, but on the whole they are kind.

Love, Jake

P.S. Do not let Max use my room.

faults.quote: and that is what comes of going on the water
faults.why: Adds a moral/verdict not in the original; Jake does not blame the water or generalise. It is more than commentary and shifts the tone from embarrassment to a lesson.

faults.quote: a charger for the instrument by which I speak with you
faults.why: The phone is turned into a circumlocution; it is a riddle-like obscuring of 'phone charger'. It also drops the sense that this is the writer's own phone, and the charger is an unnatural way to keep the fact.

faults.quote: I flipped the canoe
faults.why: Rewrite says 'my canoe turned over', removing Jake's agency, and 'went out in the canoes' blurs 'we went canoeing'. Minor shift of meaning.

faults.quote: she is very pleasant
faults.why: Original 'really cool' is a stronger, admiring feeling; 'pleasant' weakens the degree of his admiration.

faults.quote: the friend who sleeps in my room
faults.why: A 'bunkmate' becomes a 'friend', adding a relationship not stated. Also 'my room' clashes with the P.S. 'my room' at home, creating confusion between camp and home.

faults.quote: On the whole they are kind.
faults.why: 'Mostly fine' becomes 'kind', raising the warmth of the feeling beyond the original.

faults.quote: Camp is all right, I suppose, but the food is very bad
faults.why: Merges the two sentences and drops 'gross'; 'but' adds a contrast not in the original. 'Snores like crazy' becomes 'very loudly', flattening it.

faults.quote: talk about many things
faults.why: 'Stuff' is rendered vaguely; fine, but 'hang out' becomes 'sit', losing the activity. The sentence reads stiffly.

faults.quote: I was greatly ashamed
faults.why: Fairy Books diction is more plain narration with 'whereupon', 'at once', and 'said'; the first-person letter register with 'I suppose' and 'somewhat' is closer to generic Victorian than Lang's tale-telling. Little real fairy-tale cadence or marked vocabulary.

faults.quote: cites The Olive Fairy Book, “The Billy Goat And The King”, ¶ 27
faults.why: The cited sources are dubious and unverifiable; 'The Golden Branch' and 'The Fairy Of The Dawn' do not obviously support the moves claimed (e.g., 'People by their place'). The citations seem to be fabricated attributions.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Notes skip the major changes: the phone circumlocution, 'all right, I suppose', the P.S., and the added moral. The numbering by paragraph also does not match the letter's structure, since it lists six paragraphs for a letter with fewer.

faults.quote: People by their place: “the friend who sleeps in my room snores very loudly”
faults.why: The note presents 'friend' as a move, but the change is a fidelity departure and not reported as such.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is readable and mostly keeps the facts, but it adds a moral, softens some feelings, turns 'phone charger' into a riddle, and gets only a thin Fairy Book flavour. The notes cite doubtful sources and leave the largest changes unexplained.

The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.

The office into which I was shown was huge and very new, and every soul in it wore a hooded coat in place of a good coat, and drank fine coffee, but not one of them seemed to be working. I myself had come in a good suit, and I felt altogether out of place in it.

The woman who governed the place was called Priya, and she was friendly, but there was something keen and pressing in her manner. She asked me what good was in me and what weakness, and I told her I was the sort of person who does all things too well and too long for fear they should be done ill; which was a poor thing to say. Yet she smiled at me for all that.

When the interview was over I called my sister, and she said I had surely got what I went for. I hope she is in the right, for I stand in great need of this place; the rent falls due next week, and I have no money.

faults.quote: but not one of them seemed to be working
faults.why: Invented claim. The writer never said anyone was idle. This adds a new negative judgment about the staff.

faults.quote: I told her I was the sort of person who does all things too well and too long for fear they should be done ill
faults.why: The writer said only 'I was a perfectionist.' The rewrite adds an elaborate explanation of what perfectionism means, with new content.

faults.quote: super modern
faults.why: 'Super modern' is rendered as 'very new,' which loses the sense of contemporary style. Hoodies become 'a hooded coat in place of a good coat,' an added contrast that is not in the original.

faults.quote: which was a poor thing to say
faults.why: The writer called the answer a lame answer, meaning cliché. 'A poor thing to say' is a bit different, but it is acceptable. The bigger issue is the following 'Yet she smiled at me for all that,' which is fine.

faults.quote: I have no money
faults.why: 'Basically broke' is flattened to an absolute 'no money.' The writer's hedge is lost.

faults.quote: she said I had surely got what I went for
faults.why: 'Probably nailed it' becomes 'surely.' This raises the certainty and shifts the degree of the sister's confidence.

faults.quote: every soul in it wore a hooded coat in place of a good coat
faults.why: Awkward and unclear. 'Hooded coat' for a hoodie, and a 'good coat' contrast, read as a riddle.

faults.quote: She asked me what good was in me and what weakness
faults.why: Garbled phrasing. 'What good was in me' is not idiomatic for asking about strengths.

faults.quote: I called my sister
faults.why: 'Called' on the telephone is an anachronism in a fairy-book register, and the rewrite did nothing to render it, which breaks the voice.

faults.quote: The office into which I was shown
faults.why: The first-person modern interview narrative is rendered in a stiff, generic archaic style. The Fairy Books' plain, brisk narration ('Once upon a time') is not captured. The voice leans on semicolons and 'for all that' pastiche.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “and every soul in it drank fine coffee, but not one of them seemed to be working.”
faults.why: The quote does not match the rewrite text. It omits 'wore a hooded coat... and.' The move justifies an invented addition rather than reporting it.

faults.quote: too well and too long; which was a poor thing to say.
faults.why: The quote is again altered from the rewrite, which has 'for fear they should be done ill.' The notes do not report the added elaboration of perfectionism.

faults.quote: I stand in great need of it
faults.why: Misquotes the rewrite, which says 'of this place.' The 'Antithesis' label does not fit that sentence. The citations to specific tales and paragraph numbers look unsupportable for such modern content.

faults.quote: hooded coat in place of a good coat
faults.why: The rewrite adds a muddled contrast and no note explains it. Modern items like 'hoodies' and 'fancy coffee' are not clearly conveyed, which hurts clarity.

judge.verdict: The rewrite adds content (idle staff, an elaborated definition of perfectionism), inflates 'probably' to 'surely,' and has some garbled phrasing. The notes misquote the rewrite and make dubious source citations, and the voice is generic archaic pastiche rather than the plain Fairy Book narration.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Once upon a time a new family came to live in the house next door, and they brought with them a great cart and two little children. The father seemed a good man, and the woman held herself apart and spoke little, but this was by her manner and not by any unkindness.

My mother baked them cakes that very day, for she wished to learn all about them, and presently she had it all. She found out where they came from, what they did for their work, and whether they went to church. So it came out that the father was a lawyer, and that he had no wife, and that he and the children were alone in the world, his wife having parted from him.

When my mother heard this she got a look upon her face that I knew well, for she had been trying to find me a husband for years, and I saw at once that she meant to set me before this lawyer.

That least change keeps the matchmaking point: the father is available.

faults.quote: but this was by her manner and not by any unkindness
faults.why: The writer called the mom 'kind of standoffish'. This clause adds a defence of her character and softens the feeling. The writer's mild disapproval is turned into reassurance.

faults.quote: and that he and the children were alone in the world
faults.why: This invents a claim the writer never made. It also contradicts the woman who still lives in the household and the 'great cart' that carried the whole family.

faults.quote: the woman held herself apart and spoke little
faults.why: The mending is incomplete. Calling her 'the woman' never says who she is (sister, nanny, mother-in-law?), so the reader is left with an unexplained person. The note claims the later 'divorced' line makes this clear, but it does not.

faults.quote: he and the children were alone in the world, his wife having parted from him
faults.why: This undoes the mending. If the father and children are 'alone', the woman has no place in the household, and the rewrite now has its own contradiction.

faults.quote: I saw at once that she meant to set me before this lawyer
faults.why: The writer's 'I knew exactly what she was thinking' and 'set me up' are changed to 'find me a husband' and 'set me before'. This adds marriage as the aim and loses the dry weariness of 'for years'.

faults.quote: Once upon a time a new family came to live in the house next door
faults.why: A fairy-tale opening is stuck on a first-person, modern-domestic anecdote ('my mother', 'this lawyer'). The Fairy Books are third-person narration, so the register reads as costume. The 'great cart' for the truck and 'church' also sit awkwardly together.

faults.quote: he had no wife
faults.why: The writer's wry 'Well, divorced' correction is flattened into two plain clauses. The sentence 'So it came out that... and that... and that...' is clumsy and over-padded.

faults.quote: “where they came from, what they did for their bread, and whether they went to church”
faults.why: The quoted source line says 'for their bread', but the rewrite says 'for their work'. The quote does not match what was actually produced.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “for they had but one mother between them...
faults.why: The rewrite contains no ironic verdict, so this cited move names a change that was not made.

faults.quote: Periphrasis: “a look upon her face that I knew well”
faults.why: This is a plain rewording, not a periphrasis. The label is inaccurate and teaches little.

faults.quote: I made her 'the woman' rather than 'the mom'
faults.why: The notes do not report the added 'alone in the world' or 'not by any unkindness'. These are the changes that matter most, and they are not disclosed.

judge.verdict: The rewrite spots the mom/divorced contradiction but mends it badly. 'The woman' is left unexplained, and the added 'alone in the world' contradicts her, along with other softening additions. The Fairy Book flavour is thin, and several notes cite moves the text does not contain or misquote it.

The party was at Jessica's house. Her parents were out of town. Everyone from school was there and the music was super loud.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma. We didn't know many people. Then this tall guy came over and started talking to us. His name was Chris. He was kind of arrogant but also funny.

Once upon a time Jessica gave a party at her house, and her parents were away from town, and all the school was there and the music was very loud. I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we knew few of the people.

Then a tall young man came over to us and began to talk, and his name was Chris; he was proud, but he was also merry. He called the party a poor one and the people dull folk. faults.quote: he was proud, but he was also merry
faults.why: "Arrogant" becomes "proud", which is milder and partly positive. "Funny" becomes "merry", which means cheerful rather than witty. The writer's ambivalence is slightly shifted.

faults.quote: I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we knew few of the people.
faults.why: "We didn't know many people" is kept, but the "kitchen" detail and the paragraph break are handled loosely. The point is minor, since the facts survive.

faults.quote: the music was very loud
faults.why: "Super loud" is flattened to "very loud", and the emphasis is lost. The notes also call this a periphrasis, though it is a plain rendering.

faults.quote: all the school was there
faults.why: "Everyone from school" is kept, but "all the school" is slightly odd, and the "out of town" phrasing is changed to "away from town".

faults.quote: then I said to myself that perhaps I had been wrong about him
faults.why: This adds a narrated inner speech act that the writer did not have. The writer's "Maybe I was wrong" is a fleeting thought, so the shift is small but real.

faults.quote: and her parents were away from town, and all the school was there and the music was very loud
faults.why: A run of "and" clauses is a plausible Lang move. But the first-person narrator with "I said to myself" is not how the Fairy Books narrate. They are third-person tales, so the rewrite sounds like a costume more than the real texts.

faults.quote: the people dull folk
faults.why: The phrasing is slightly stilted and does not read as idiomatic Lang. "Called the party a poor one" is also awkward.

faults.quote: he was proud, but he was also merry
faults.why: The semicolon-and-antithesis construction is clumsy. "Merry" does not suit a sarcastic, rude guy who calls the party lame.

faults.quote: set the house in order when all the rest had gone away
faults.why: It is fine as pastiche but wordy. "Helping to set the house in order" is a little too tidy for "clean up".

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “said this young man, who plainly thought a great deal of himself” — cites The Brown Fairy Book
faults.why: The quoted sentence does not appear in the rewrite, so this note describes a change that was not made. It is a fabricated or misattributed move.

faults.quote: Antithesis: “he was proud, but he was also merry” — cites The Yellow Fairy Book, “The Grateful Beasts(11)”, ¶ 2
faults.why: The citation is dubious. The notes also repeat the same sentence under several labels, so they teach little.

faults.quote: Periphrasis: “the music was very loud”
faults.why: This is not periphrasis. It is a direct, nearly literal rendering, so the label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Paragraph 1 (renders the writer’s ¶1, 2)
faults.why: The rewrite merges the writer's three paragraphs into two. The notes admit this, but the merge is not needed and the paragraph mapping is muddled, since paragraph 2 is said to render the writer's ¶2, 3 while paragraph 1 already used ¶2.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and has a pleasant fairy-tale opening, but it shifts "arrogant" and "funny" to "proud" and "merry", adds a narrated "said to myself", and uses a first-person frame that Lang's tales lack. The notes are weak: one cites a quotation that does not appear in the rewrite, and others mislabel plain phrases as moves.

I needed milk. So I grabbed my keys and drove to the store. It was super crowded. A guy in a hoodie was blocking the whole aisle while he talked on his phone.

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid and left as fast as I could. Honestly, it was the most awkward ten minutes of my week.
rewrite:
I was in want of milk, so I caught up my keys and drove to the store.

There were so many people in the store that a man in his hooded jacket stood the whole length of the aisle, talking into his little instrument, and would not let me pass. I did not wish to be rude, so I said, "Excuse me"; but he paid me no heed, and talked on. In the end he moved aside, and I took the milk. And then I saw my old sweetheart at the check, and my heart stood still with fear.

"Hey," said she, "it is long since we have met; you look very well."

"I thank you," said I, "and you the same."; and I paid and went out as fast as ever I could. And if a man is in want of milk, he may well meet every soul he does not wish to meet.

And then I saw my old sweetheart at the check, and my heart stood still with fear.

faults.quote: And if a man is in want of milk, he may well meet every soul he does not wish to meet.
faults.why: This replaces the writer's closing judgment ('the most awkward ten minutes of my week') with an invented general moral. The 'awkward' feeling, the 'ten minutes' and the 'my week' are all lost. 'Every soul' also exaggerates, since only one person was met.

faults.quote: There were so many people in the store that a man in his hooded jacket stood the whole length of the aisle
faults.why: The 'so many ... that' construction makes the crowd the cause of the man blocking the aisle. The original says only that it was crowded and that a man was blocking the aisle. This adds a false causal link, and 'stood the whole length' is unclear.

faults.quote: stood the whole length of the aisle
faults.why: A man cannot stand 'the whole length' of an aisle. The phrase is awkward and nearly nonsensical where 'blocked the whole aisle' was meant.

faults.quote: "I thank you," said I, "and you the same."; and I paid
faults.why: The punctuation '.";' is wrong. A closing quote followed by a semicolon after a full stop is a typographical garble.

faults.quote: at the check
faults.why: 'The check' for the checkout is not idiomatic and may read as a bill or a cheque. It is unclear and does not sound like Lang.

faults.quote: my old sweetheart
faults.why: The writer says 'my ex', meaning a former partner after a breakup. 'Old sweetheart' softens this and loses the sense of a failed relationship.

faults.quote: "Hey," said she
faults.why: 'Hey' is a modern interjection in an otherwise archaic register. It sits as modern prose in costume, and 'Hey' is not a Fairy Book greeting.

faults.quote: my heart stood still with fear
faults.why: The writer says 'basically panicked', a casual, hedged reaction. 'Stood still with fear' is a stronger, differently coloured feeling, nearer to terror than awkward panic.

faults.quote: My old sweetheart stood at the check, and my heart stood still with fear.
faults.why: The note quotes a sentence that is not in the rewrite. The rewrite reads 'And then I saw my old sweetheart at the check, and my heart stood still with fear.' The quotation is misreported.

faults.quote: The happy ending: “And if a man is in want of milk
faults.why: The line is an invented moral, not a happy ending. The note does not tell the writer that the original closing sentence was replaced and its content dropped.

faults.quote: Paragraph 4 (renders the writer’s ¶4)
faults.why: The notes assume four paragraphs, but the rewrite's dialogue and closing moral share one paragraph. The structure notes are vague, and the rewrite changed the paragraphing without saying so.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the main events and has some fitting Lang-like phrasing ('in want of', 'said she', 'paid me no heed'). It garbles the aisle sentence, drops the 'most awkward ten minutes' ending in favour of an invented moral, and has a punctuation slip. The notes misquote the text and call the moral a 'happy ending'.

faults.quote: They are ever the slowest to set their hand to any page, as all the company knows.
faults.why: Invented sentence: it adds a new, sarcastic claim that legal is always slow and that everyone knows it. The original only said legal has not yet signed off. This also changes the feeling, since Sam is neutral and the rewrite blames Legal.

faults.quote: Quick update: the launch is moving
faults.why: The rewrite renders 'launch' as 'the sending forth' and later 'send the thing forth'. This loses the product-launch meaning and 'shipping' is blurred into the same phrase. 'The sending forth' is vague about what is being sent.

faults.quote: Those who mind the law
faults.why: 'Legal' is a team or department. Rendering it as 'those who mind the law' is a loose paraphrase that loses the sense of a specific group, though it is passable.

faults.quote: Let each of you have his share of the writing done
faults.why: The deck, as a presentation, is lost: 'the writing' does not say 'deck'. 'His share' also genders the team, though this is in keeping with the voice.

faults.quote: Good day to you, my team,
faults.why: A stiff, generic archaic greeting. The Fairy Books do not open with such a salutation, and the voice does not sustain 'Good day' with the 'Here is a word of news' that follows. The result is pastiche more than Lang's plain, brisk narration.

faults.quote: I thank you, Sam.
faults.why: An awkward sign-off that keeps the name on the same line as the thanks. It reads as a costume rather than a fairy-tale cadence, and the signature is not set apart.

faults.quote: if any of you is stayed
faults.why: 'Stayed' for 'blocked' is an odd usage; the sense of 'delayed or hindered' is archaic but unclear, and may read as 'stopped' or 'supported'.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “They are ever the slowest to set their hand to any page, as all the company knows.”
faults.why: The note presents an invented sentence as a stylistic move and does not report it as an addition that changes the meaning. It also cites a specific paragraph of 'Heart Of Ice' that is unlikely to contain such a verdict.

faults.quote: Things in threes: “the sending forth goes from Tuesday to Thursday; let each of you have his share of the writing done by noon on Wednesday; and if any of you is stayed, let him say so today and not tomorrow”
faults.why: The quoted text is not what appears in the rewrite: it is stitched together from separate paragraphs and punctuation is altered. These items are not a real triple in the draft; they are three separate points, so the note misdescribes the change.

faults.quote: And so, and then: “and if any of you is stayed, let him say so today, and not tomorrow”
faults.why: The 'and so, and then' move is not shown: the quoted clause has no 'and then' sequencing. The same sentence is cited for two different moves, which is padding. The notes also omit the real changes (the 'Legal' paraphrase, the 'launch' paraphrase, the invented insult).

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 1 and 4 receive no notes although the greeting and sign-off were heavily changed.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the dates and requests but invents a snide line about Legal, which alters the feeling and adds a fact. The voice is a thin archaic costume, and the notes misquote the text and do not report the addition.
