Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: On Saturday I cleaned the troughs of the roof, and I mended the sink that let the water through, and I called my old grandmother, who talked for an hour together about her neighbour's cat. By the evening I was weary, but I was proud of myself all the same.

rows.text: On Saturday I cleaned the troughs of the roof, and I mended the sink that let the water through, and I called my old grandmother, who talked for an hour together about her neighbour's cat. By the evening I was weary, but I was proud of myself all the same.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

faults.quote: I was weary, but I was proud of myself all the same.
faults.why: Drops 'weirdly'. The writer's slight surprise at feeling proud is lost, and 'exhausted' is softened to 'weary'. The feeling is flattened.

faults.quote: my old grandmother
faults.why: The writer never said she was old. 'Old' is an added detail, though a mild one.

faults.quote: the sink that let the water through
faults.why: 'Leaky' becomes a paraphrase that could mean the sink let water drain through, which is its job. It is a little ambiguous and over-periphrastic.

faults.quote: cleaned the troughs of the roof
faults.why: A riddling periphrasis for 'gutters'. Lang would more likely write 'gutters' or 'the water-spouts'. It reads as a thesaurus swap, not idiom.

faults.quote: talked for an hour together
faults.why: 'Together' is a stray filler. Nobody else is talking, so it reads oddly.

faults.quote: On Saturday I cleaned ... and I mended ... and I called
faults.why: The Fairy Books are narrated in third person past, with 'Once upon a time' framing and plain narrative diction. A first-person diary list with 'and I' repeated is only thinly Langian. 'Called' (phone) is anachronistic and was left unadapted, and the weak 'all the same' tag carries little flavour.

faults.quote: cites The Lilac Fairy Book, “The Enchanted Deer”, ¶ 40
faults.why: The citations look unverifiable and the paragraph numbers are suspect. The 'things in threes' move is also not what the rewrite does: the writer's list was already three items, and nothing was added.

faults.quote: People by their place: “my old grandmother”
faults.why: This mislabels the change. 'Old' is just an added adjective, and nothing identifies a person by their place or role beyond what the writer gave.

faults.quote: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The merge is stated, but the notes do not mention the changes to 'weirdly' and 'exhausted' or the invented 'old'. They teach little about what was lost.

judge.verdict: A faithful skeleton, but the rewrite loses 'weirdly' and 'exhausted', adds 'old', and uses awkward periphrases ('troughs of the roof', 'together'). The voice is only lightly Langian and the notes' moves and citations are doubtful.

I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite: I have never seen Paris. The last time I was there the rain fell the whole week through, and on the second day my brother lost his passport. So we passed nearly all the journey at the embassy. He says still that it was the best holiday he ever had.

rows.text: I have never seen Paris. The last time I was there the rain fell the whole week through, and on the second day my brother lost his passport. So we passed nearly all the journey at the embassy. He says still that it was the best holiday he ever had.

notes.text: Your first sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris, but the next sentence describes the narrator's last time there, and the pair spending most of the trip at the embassy, so the narrator has in fact been to Paris. I changed 'been' to 'seen': the narrator was in the city but never experienced it, which agrees with the rainy week and the embassy stay, and keeps the point that the trip was no proper visit.
notes.after: I have never seen Paris.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: I have never seen Paris.
So we passed nearly all the journey at the embassy.
notes.cite: The Olive Fairy Book, “The Prince And Princess In The Forest”, ¶ 137

notes.after: on the second day my brother lost his passport
the rain fell the whole week through
notes.cite: The Violet Fairy Book, “A Tale Of The Tontlawald”, ¶ 3

faults.quote: I have never seen Paris. The last time I was there
faults.why: The mend is reported, but it is only partly consistent. 'The last time' still implies several visits, which sits oddly with 'never seen'. The note does not say that this reading is a guess, and it does not offer the alternative that the contradiction is a joke.

faults.quote: He says still that it was the best holiday he ever had.
faults.why: 'Says still' is a stiff, pseudo-archaic inversion that no fairy-book narrator would use. 'He still says' is the natural form. It reads as costume rather than idiom.

faults.quote: we passed nearly all the journey at the embassy
faults.why: 'Trip' became 'journey', and 'most of' became 'nearly all'. Both shift the sense slightly. A journey is the travelling, not the stay in Paris, so 'passed the journey at the embassy' is a little off.

faults.quote: The last time I was there the rain fell the whole week through, and on the second day my brother lost his passport.
faults.why: This is plain modern prose with a few word swaps. It lacks Lang's fairy-tale markers: 'Now', 'it came to pass', the 'and so' chaining, a tale-teller's framing. The first-person modern anecdote is hardly transformed.

faults.quote: Litotes: “the rain fell the whole week through”
faults.why: This is not litotes, which is understatement by negation. It is a plain hyperbolic duration phrase, so the label teaches the wrong thing.

faults.quote: People by their place: “on the second day my brother lost his passport”
faults.why: The sentence names a time and an event, not a person defined by their place or station. The move label does not match the quoted text.

faults.quote: Once upon a time: “I have never seen Paris.”
faults.why: The sentence has no 'once upon a time' opening feature. The cited move is a stretch, and the source is not apt for a first-person statement of experience.

faults.quote: Structure: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
faults.why: The merge is reported, but it loses the writer's paragraph break before the punchline about the embassy. The note does not explain why the merge helps.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the 'never been' contradiction and reports the mend, but the mend is only partly consistent and not flagged as a guess. The voice is thin and the phrasing is awkward in places ('says still'). Several move labels in the notes are inaccurate or invented, so they teach little.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

When Dana scratched our dinner, I was not sorry at all, for I was truly glad of it. And I had been dreading it all the week long, and that I am not proud to own.

'It is well, and we will do it another time,' said I; but I do not think we ever shall.

rows.text: 'It is well, and we will do it another time,' said I; but I do not think we ever shall.

notes.text: Your ending lightly echoes the promise-made-lightly motif of Rumpelstiltskin and The Frog Prince: the narrator tells Dana 'we'd do it another time' and at once knows the promise is hollow — 'I don't think we will.' The rewrite keeps the promise hollow, as your narrator truly means to drop the dinner, and makes its hollow ring plain with 'but I do not think we ever shall'; it does not make the promise binding.

faults.quote: for I was truly glad of it
faults.why: The writer said 'relieved'; 'truly glad' makes the feeling more positive, and it adds a redundant clause. It also reads as a reason for the preceding clause rather than an intensification, which blurs the original.

faults.quote: 'It is well, and we will do it another time,' said I
faults.why: The writer reports the speech indirectly ('I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time'). The rewrite makes it direct speech with no mention of telling Dana, so the addressee is lost. 'It is well' is also a weaker match for 'it's fine'.

faults.quote: scratched our dinner
faults.why: 'Scratched' is a modern idiom for cancelling, as in scratching an event. It is not fairy-book diction and is slightly ambiguous. Something like 'put off' or 'begged to be excused' would fit better, and 'put off' would also be accurate.

faults.quote: all the week long, and that I am not proud to own
faults.why: 'all the week long' is awkward, and the dangling 'and that I am not proud to own' is stilted rather than idiomatic. 'And' is repeated three times in the paragraph, which sounds mechanical.

faults.quote: I was not sorry at all, for I was truly glad of it
faults.why: Lang's fairy books rarely use this reflective first-person confessional register. The passage sounds like generic archaic pastiche rather than the plain, brisk narration of the tales.

faults.quote: cites The Green Fairy Book, “The War Of The Wolf And The Fox”, ¶ 7
faults.why: The cited line is the rewrite's own sentence, not a quotation from the source. The note presents a generic 'and so, and then' connective as a named move, and it is not evidently apt for a sentence about dreading.

faults.quote: Your ending lightly echoes the promise-made-lightly motif of Rumpelstiltskin and The Frog Prince
faults.why: This is a forced comparison with irrelevant tales. The note is labelled 'sense' but reports no real mending, and it is confusing about what changed. Its closing remark that the rewrite 'does not make the promise binding' is irrelevant.

faults.quote: The happy ending: “but I do not think we ever shall.”
faults.why: Mislabelled: the line is a doubtful, bleak ending, not a happy ending. The cited source (Little King Loc) is dubious for it.

faults.quote: but I do not think we ever shall
faults.why: The writer says 'I don't think we will'; 'ever' strengthens it to near-certainty. This is a slight shift in degree.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent a writing unto me, saying, We must needs talk: and he said that we should talk together. And I knew even then what that word meant.

And it came to pass on the next day, that we met together at a house in the city where they sold drink; and he was there before me, and his eyes were upon his phone, and he handled it. And his countenance was troubled, and he was sore afraid. And he said unto me that he was not ready for a thing so grave and so solemn, and that it was not I, but he: the fault, he said, lay in him, and not in me.

And I would have wept, but I wept not: and I bowed mine head, and I said, It is well. Then I went home on foot in the rain; and I ate a whole vessel of ice cream, and left nothing of it: a fine comfort, and a man might do worse.

And she that dwelt with me said in her heart that I grieved more than the matter was worth. Perhaps I did. But it hurt me still.

faults.quote: saying, We must needs talk: and he said that we should talk together.
faults.why: The original has a text saying they need to talk. The rewrite says the same thing twice, which is redundant filler and adds a second speech act.

faults.quote: he was sore afraid
faults.why: The original says 'He looked nervous'. 'Sore afraid' overstates it, and 'troubled' is also added, so the feeling is intensified.

faults.quote: and he handled it
faults.why: He was 'scrolling', and 'handled' is a vague, odd substitute. It also adds something not in the original.

faults.quote: a fine comfort, and a man might do worse
faults.why: This is an invented commentary. It changes the writer's tone, since the original has no wry approval of the ice cream. 'A man' is also out of place for a female narrator.

faults.quote: said in her heart that I grieved more than the matter was worth
faults.why: The roommate 'thought I was overreacting'. The rewrite makes it 'grieved', which is not quite overreacting, and adds 'the matter was worth'. 'Said in her heart' is acceptable but the shift is real.

faults.quote: a thing so grave and so solemn
faults.why: Original: 'something serious'. The doubled adjectives inflate it into grandeur and change the degree of feeling.

faults.quote: a house in the city where they sold drink
faults.why: This is an awkward circumlocution for a coffee shop. 'Drink' suggests alcohol rather than coffee, and 'downtown' is flattened to 'in the city'.

faults.quote: I would have wept, but I wept not: and I bowed mine head
faults.why: 'Would have wept, but wept not' is clumsy. It also loses the nodding, since 'bowed my head' differs from nodding in assent. The sequence 'I went home on foot' is stilted.

faults.quote: a whole vessel of ice cream
faults.why: The 'pint' becomes a 'vessel', which is unidiomatic and unintentionally comic. 'And left nothing of it' is also an addition.

faults.quote: But it hurt me still.
faults.why: This is plain modern prose, not KJV cadence, and it breaks the register of the rest. 'Perhaps I did' is also modern.

faults.quote: And it came to pass on the next day
faults.why: The 'came to pass' formula is applied mechanically and repeatedly. KJV would vary with 'And on the morrow' or 'Then', and the paragraphs are not built with real parallelism.

faults.quote: Then I went home on foot in the rain
faults.why: The original says 'walked home in the rain'. This is acceptable, but it omits that the rain and the walk are tied to her emotional state, and the last paragraph's tone is changed.

faults.quote: cites Ruth 3:8
faults.why: The citations look arbitrary or invented. The cited verses do not exemplify the quoted construction, such as Mark 13:35 for 'the genitive with of', when the quoted sentence has no genitive 'of' construction.

faults.quote: Behold, lo, verily: “And his countenance was troubled, and he was sore afraid.”
faults.why: The label names behold, lo and verily, but none of these appears in the example. The same mismatch is found in 'Unto, thereof, wherefore', where 'thereof' and 'wherefore' are absent.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “And I would have wept, but I wept not.” — cites 2 Samuel 22:42
faults.why: This is not an accurate example of the cited parallelism, and the notes do not report any sense changes or the added commentary.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a KJV flavor from 'it came to pass' and archaic pronouns, but it duplicates and inflates details, adds an invented aside about the ice cream, and uses clumsy circumlocutions ('vessel', 'house where they sold drink'). The notes mislabel moves and cite verses that do not fit.

Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Unto my father and my mother, greeting.

The camp is well enough, as I suppose; the food thereof is not to my liking, and he that lieth in the same place with me maketh a noise in his sleeping all the night long. And it came to pass yesterday that we went forth in a canoe upon the water, and I turned it over, and all they that were with me laughed me to scorn: and my countenance fell, for I was sore ashamed.

But there is a damsel among the company, whose name is Kayla, which is truly a good companion: she is of Ohio, and in the matter of horses there is none that knoweth more than she. We sit us down by the lake after the evening meal, and we talk one with another of many matters. And I think that she hath a liking toward me, but I am not sure of it.

Can ye send unto me more of such things as I may eat? And the charger of my phone also, which I wholly left behind me; for the counsellors are somewhat exact with us, yet for the most part they are well enough.

The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand.

Moreover, I beseech you, suffer not Max to use my room.

faults.quote: which I wholly left behind me; for the counsellors are somewhat exact with us
faults.why: The writer's phone charger and the counselors' strictness are separate points. Joining them with 'for' makes strictness the reason for forgetting the charger, which the original does not say.

faults.quote: The camp is well enough, as I suppose;
faults.why: 'Okay I guess' is rendered weakly. 'Gross' food becomes merely 'not to my liking', which understates the disgust.

faults.quote: snores like crazy
faults.why: The intensity is reduced to 'maketh a noise in his sleeping all the night long'. It no longer names snoring and gives no sense of extremity.

faults.quote: truly a good companion
faults.why: 'Really cool' becomes 'good companion', which loses the sense of admiration or attraction. 'Truly' is not the writer's emphasis.

faults.quote: The salutation of me Jake with mine own hand.
faults.why: This is a Pauline closing formula that replaces 'Love, Jake'. The affection of the original is lost.

faults.quote: Moreover, I beseech you, suffer not Max to use my room.
faults.why: The P.S. has become a main-text sentence, so its afterthought quality is lost. The 'P.S.' is dropped.

faults.quote: which is truly a good companion
faults.why: 'Whose name is Kayla, which is truly a good companion' has a clumsy relative: 'which' is used of a person and the clause is awkward.

faults.quote: and the charger of my phone also
faults.why: 'Phone' is left as a bare modern word inside an archaic frame. The 'ye' and 'unto me' sit awkwardly beside 'Can ye send', which is a modern question form.

faults.quote: Can ye send unto me more of such things as I may eat?
faults.why: Fronted 'Can ye' is not KJV syntax. KJV would use 'Send unto me, I pray you, more...'. It also switches from the 'my father and my mother' address, which is a minor inconsistency.

faults.quote: Unto my father and my mother, greeting.
faults.why: The frame is plausible, but the register is mostly generic 'thee/ye' pastiche rather than distinctive KJV rhythm. Kayla's paragraph in particular is flat.

faults.quote: cites Acts 16:16
faults.why: Acts 16:16 is not an apt or accurate source for 'And it came to pass'. The same applies to the other citations (Luke 15:32, Exodus 5:11, Hebrews 4:16, Philippians 3:15, 1 Corinthians 10:27), which look arbitrary and do not illustrate the named moves.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “the counsellors are somewhat exact with us...
faults.why: The quoted sentence has no thou/thee or -eth/-est forms, so the note does not match the text. The notes also omit the sign-off changes, the P.S. restructuring and the sentence merging.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The salutation, the sign-off and the restructured P.S. are real changes that go unreported.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is readable and mostly faithful in events, but it flattens feeling, such as 'gross' and 'really cool'. It also invents a causal link between the charger and the counselors, and it replaces 'Love' with a Pauline formula. The notes carry mismatched, dubious citations and one note describes forms that are not in the quoted line.

The office was huge and super modern. Everyone wore hoodies and drank fancy coffee. I felt totally out of place in my suit.

The manager was a woman named Priya. She was friendly but kind of intense. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses. I said I was a perfectionist, which is a lame answer. She smiled anyway.

After the interview I called my sister. She said I probably nailed it. I hope she's right because I really need this job. Rent is due next week and I'm basically broke.
rewrite:
And the office was exceeding great and new; and every one that was therein had hoodies upon him, and drank coffee. And I felt in my heart that I had no place among them, being clad in my suit.

And the woman that ruled over the office was named Priya, and she was friendly, but of an earnest and fierce countenance. And she asked of me my strengths and my weaknesses; and I said unto her, I am one that will do all things wholly and perfectly: and this was a lame answer. And yet she set a pleasant look upon me.

And it came to pass after the interview, that I called my sister; and she said, Peradventure it hath gone well with thee. And I hope she speaketh truly, for I have sore need of this job: for the rent falleth due in the week that cometh, and I have no money left unto me.

faults.quote: exceeding great and new
faults.why: 'Super modern' becomes plain 'new', which loses the contemporary, cutting-edge sense.

faults.quote: drank coffee
faults.why: 'Fancy' is dropped, so the writer's slightly mocking note on the coffee is lost.

faults.quote: the woman that ruled over the office
faults.why: 'Manager' becomes one who 'ruled over' the office, which overstates her role.

faults.quote: of an earnest and fierce countenance
faults.why: 'Kind of intense' is hedged and mild. 'Fierce' overstates it, and the 'kind of' softening is gone.

faults.quote: I am one that will do all things wholly and perfectly
faults.why: The writer said 'I said I was a perfectionist', reported speech naming the cliché answer. The rewrite turns it into a paraphrase in direct speech, and the word 'perfectionist' is lost.

faults.quote: And yet she set a pleasant look upon me.
faults.why: 'She smiled anyway' becomes a vague 'pleasant look', and the smile itself is lost.

faults.quote: Peradventure it hath gone well with thee.
faults.why: The sister said 'I probably nailed it'. This is a vaguer 'it hath gone well', and the confident, colloquial sense of 'nailed' is weakened.

faults.quote: I have no money left unto me
faults.why: 'Basically broke' is hedged. The rewrite makes it absolute and drops the 'basically'.

faults.quote: and this was a lame answer
faults.why: In the KJV 'lame' means crippled, so the modern slang sense reads oddly. The rewrite also leaves the writer's present-tense 'is' and adds an awkward explanatory 'and'.

faults.quote: And I hope she speaketh truly
faults.why: 'I hope' is a modern construction beside the archaic verb, and the sentence stacks 'for... for...' clumsily.

faults.quote: had hoodies upon him, and drank coffee
faults.why: The phrasing is stilted, and 'hoodies' stays as modern vocabulary in costume. The passage leans on 'And' and 'unto' but has little of the KJV's rhythm and parallelism.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “every one that was therein had hoodies upon him”
faults.why: The quoted sentence contains no genitive with 'of', so the label does not describe it, and the Matthew 1:18 citation is not apt.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “And yet she set a pleasant look upon me.”
faults.why: The sentence contains none of unto, thereof or wherefore, so the label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “I am one that will do all things wholly and perfectly: and this was a lame answer.” — cites Mark 7:11
faults.why: Mark 7:11 (Corban) is not an apt model for a self-judging aside. The 'ironic verdict' is also not a KJV move, so the citation looks arbitrary.

faults.quote: cites Luke 10:39
faults.why: The cited verse is loosely matched to 'and... and' parataxis. Some other citations, such as Luke 13:12 and Luke 8:47, are also not clearly tied to the moves they are cited for.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a plausible KJV flavor (and, unto, it came to pass), but it drops 'fancy' and 'modern', overstates Priya as 'fierce' and 'ruled over', and flattens 'smiled' and 'perfectionist'. The notes mislabel moves and cite verses that do not fit them.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next door beside us. And they have a great cart, and two little kids. The father seemeth a good man; but the sister of the man is somewhat aloof, and keepeth herself apart.

And my mother straightway baked them cakes, and carried them over; for she desired to learn all things of them: whence they came, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.

And it was found that the father is a man of the law, and he is single; yea, he is put away from his wife. And my mother set a look upon her face, and I knew what was in her heart; for many years she hath sought to give me in marriage, and hath found no taker.

notes.text: The first paragraph gives the new family a mother, but the last says the father is single, divorced. The two cannot both hold if the woman is his wife. I made the standoffish woman his sister, so the father stays single and divorced, and the matchmaking at the end still works.

faults.quote: and hath found no taker
faults.why: The writer never says the mother's matchmaking failed or that the narrator is unmarriageable. This is an invented, mildly insulting claim, and it also shifts the feeling from wry resignation to mockery.

faults.quote: a great cart
faults.why: The writer's 'huge truck' becomes a cart. This is a period swap that changes the object, and 'great' is a weaker equivalent for 'huge'.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house next door beside us.
faults.why: 'Last weekend' is dropped, so the timing is lost. 'Next door beside us' is redundant.

faults.quote: and carried them over
faults.why: This adds an action. The writer says only that the mother baked the cookies.

faults.quote: he is put away from his wife
faults.why: 'Put away' is KJV idiom for divorce, but this passive phrasing is ambiguous about who ended the marriage. It also leaves the link between her look and setting the narrator up with him only implied.

faults.quote: the sister of the man is somewhat aloof
faults.why: The mending is acceptable and reported, but it is a guess. It also leaves the two little kids with no mother, and 'sister of the man' appears from nowhere without any introduction.

faults.quote: And they have a great cart, and two little kids. The father seemeth a good man
faults.why: Tenses jump from past narrative ('came to dwell') to present ('have', 'seemeth', 'is single'). The slang 'little kids' also sits oddly in KJV diction.

faults.quote: my mother set a look upon her face
faults.why: This is an unidiomatic construction for the KJV, which would say something like 'her countenance changed'. It reads as a stiff calque of 'got this look'.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “And the father is a man of the law, and he is single; yea, he is put away from his wife.” — cites Mark 14:8
faults.why: The label does not match the example, which has no thou/thee/-eth/-est. The quoted line also differs from the rewrite, which begins 'And it was found that the father…'. Mark 14:8 ('She hath done what she could') is not an apt source.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “The father seemeth a good man; but the sister of the man is somewhat aloof, and keepeth herself apart.” — cites Acts 9:40
faults.why: Acts 9:40 (Peter raising Tabitha) is not a source for this contrast. The quoted sentence also differs from the rewrite, which says 'a good man' and 'a great cart'.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “for many years she hath sought to give me in marriage, and hath found no taker.” — cites John 16:21
faults.why: John 16:21 is about a woman in travail and has no ironic verdict. The note also does not flag the added 'found no taker' as something beyond the writer's text.

faults.quote: cites Genesis 39:13
faults.why: The source is loosely apt for 'it came to pass', but the quoted opening misquotes the rewrite, and the notes never mention changes like truck to cart or cookies to cakes.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches and reports the divorced-father/mother contradiction, and its KJV cadence is mostly convincing. But it invents 'found no taker', changes truck to cart, mixes tenses, and the notes cite mismatched verses and misquote the rewrite.

faults.quote: so that we laughed at his words: and he was not so ill a man as I had thought.
faults.why: Invents an incident (they laughed at his words) and gives the narrator's later conclusion about Chris too early, which pre-empts the ending. The original says only that he was funny.

faults.quote: and he was not so ill a man as I had thought.
faults.why: The narrator's revised opinion belongs at the end, after the cleaning. Placing it here gives the story a contradictory order: she has already revised her view, yet she next 'thought in my heart that the man was rude'.

faults.quote: and he was not so ill a man as I had thought. ... And I thought in my heart that the man was rude.
faults.why: The rewrite introduces a contradiction: the narrator has already thought better of him, and then thinks him rude. It also makes the final 'Peradventure I judged him too hastily' redundant. No note reports this.

faults.quote: And Emma lifted up her eyes.
faults.why: 'Rolled her eyes' is contempt or exasperation. 'Lifted up her eyes' in the KJV means looking up, often in prayer or at something seen, so the gesture is lost. The meaning is changed.

faults.quote: I saw him stooping and setting the house in order
faults.why: Drops the detail that everyone else had left and that it was cleaning up. The 'when all the rest were departed' clause keeps part of it, but 'but later' (the contrast with rudeness) is weakened. 'Everyone from school' is also reduced to 'all that were of the school'.

faults.quote: Peradventure I judged him too hastily.
faults.why: The original is the tentative 'Maybe I was wrong about him', but this states the verdict flatly ('judged him too hastily'), which is firmer than the writer's uncertainty.

faults.quote: The feast was at the house of Jessica
faults.why: 'Feast' makes the party into a banquet, a change of register. 'Gone out of the town' and 'the room' for kitchen are loose, and 'the room' loses the kitchen.

faults.quote: heavy and dull

faults.quote: neither was my spirit heavy at the losing of the dinner
faults.why: This adds a second restatement of 'not upset' and recasts the cancellation as 'losing' the dinner. That suggests the dinner was a loss, which fits poorly with the writer's relief and dread.

faults.quote: It is well with me; and we will take the dinner again at another time.
faults.why: The writer said 'it was fine and we'd do it another time.' The rewrite turns that into a direct promise, 'we will take the dinner', and changes the reported speech into a quoted line. 'It is well with me' also shifts the meaning slightly from 'it's fine'.

faults.quote: But I think not that we shall.
faults.why: This is acceptable in meaning, but 'we shall' now refers back to 'will take the dinner' and loses 'I don't think we will' as a plain rueful aside. The tone is weaker.

faults.quote: Verily, I was eased. for I had feared it the week through
faults.why: A lowercase 'for' follows a full stop, which is a punctuation error. 'Eased' is an odd choice for 'relieved'. 'Feared' also overstates 'dreaded', and 'the week through' is not idiomatic KJV.

faults.quote: Verily, I was eased.
faults.why: 'Verily' is used as a decorative tag. In the KJV it introduces a solemn assertion ('Verily I say unto you'), not a personal confession of relief. The sentence sounds like pastiche.

faults.quote: I am not proud of that.
faults.why: This stays in modern idiom. The KJV would use something like 'I am not proud thereof' or 'I am ashamed.' The 'did put off' construction is also more Tudor than KJV, and 'the putting off of it' is clunky.

faults.quote: cites Numbers 33:56
faults.why: This verse ('it shall come to pass, that I shall do unto you, as I thought to do unto them') is a weak and arbitrary source for the 'came to pass' opener. Many verses would fit better, such as Gen 4:3.

faults.quote: cites Luke 12:40
faults.why: This verse ('Be ye therefore ready also') has no negative-neither parallelism. The citation does not support the move.

faults.quote: cites Mark 9:12
faults.why: This is a poor example of 'verily'. The common usage is 'Verily I say unto you', for example Matt 5:18.

faults.quote: cites John 9:4
faults.why: The verse ('I must work the works of him that sent me') does not show the 'the Xing of it' genitive construction claimed.

faults.quote: cites Judges 8:2
faults.why: Judges 8:2 begins 'And he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you?' It is a loose fit for the reported-speech pattern, though it does contain 'said unto'. The notes also flag no mending and no structural changes, such as the doubled clause that was added.

judge.verdict: The meaning of relief and dread is mostly preserved, but a redundant 'neither' clause is added and the dinner is cast as a loss. The diction is mixed KJV pastiche with a punctuation slip. The source citations in the notes are largely inapt or fabricated-looking.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Camp is okay, I guess. The food is not very good, and my friend makes an awful noise every night when he is lying there. Yesterday we went out on the water, and I turned the boat over, and everybody made fun of me. It was not the finest moment of my staying here, that is for sure.

But here's the thing — there is a girl here named Kayla, and she is someone I really like. She is from Ohio, and she knows more about horses than just about anybody I have ever met. We sit by the lake after dinner and talk about everything under the sun. I think she likes me, but I cannot be sure.

Could you send me some more things to eat? And the device for my phone, which I forgot to bring along. The counselors keep a close watch on us, but they are mostly all right.

Love, Jake

I didn't want to be rude. I said excuse me. He totally ignored me. Finally he moved and I got the milk. Then I saw my ex at the checkout and I basically panicked.

Here's the thing — I needed milk. So I reached for my keys and drove down to the store. It was packed. And there, in the middle of the aisle, a man in a hoodie stood deep in a phone call, blocking the way.

We've all been there: you don't want to be rude, but you do need to get by. So I said, "Excuse me." He didn't so much as look up. Finally he moved aside — not because he'd heard me, but because he'd finished his call — and I got the milk. Then, at the register, I saw a face I wasn't ready for — the woman I used to be with.

"Hey," she said. "Long time no see. You look great."

"Thanks," I said. "You too." I paid, I picked up the milk, and I left as fast as I could. The most awkward ten minutes of my week. And all that, for a carton of milk.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
At midnight Ryan sent me word that we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant. There was no use in asking a person what a thing like that meant when he had been studying to say it at midnight, because a man don't take the trouble to say it at that hour unless it is a thing he can't keep shut of by daylight.

The next day we met at a coffee-house downtown, and he was already there, busy with his telephone, and he looked mighty nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him—which is a thing a person always says when it is him.

I wanted to cry, but I didn't; I just nodded my head and said all right, because that is about all a body can do when a man has took the trouble to tell her it is him. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream, and there ain't any better comfort in this world when a body is feeling low, only a body keeps on feeling low just the same.

My roommate said I was carrying on more than the case called for, and she judged I was making too much of it; and maybe I was. But it still hurt.

faults.quote: because a man don't take the trouble to say it at that hour unless it is a thing he can't keep shut of by daylight
faults.why: Garbled and hard to parse. 'Keep shut of' is an inverted idiom, and the logic is muddled. It also doesn't fit: the narrator is a woman using 'a man' as a generality.

faults.quote: because that is about all a body can do when a man has took the trouble to tell her it is him
faults.why: The logic doesn't connect: why does telling her 'it is him' leave her nothing to do but nod? The 'took the trouble' phrase is reused from paragraph 1 and reads as a tic.

faults.quote: he looked mighty nervous
faults.why: The Huck Finn dialect ('mighty', 'ain't', 'has took') is pasted over a modern woman's story, and the dialect is applied inconsistently, with 'coffee-house' and 'telephone' next to it. It reads as costume. Twain's own humorous essay voice would suit better than Huck's.

faults.quote: which is a thing a person always says when it is him.
faults.why: The joke is a muddled tautology. The intended point, that 'it's not you, it's me' is a polite lie, isn't clearly delivered, and it risks reading as the opposite.

faults.why: The same sentence is cited to two different sources for two labels (Huck ch. 31 and Roughing It ch. 7). The citations look arbitrary and unverifiable, and the moves named (cumulative sentence, deadpan) don't match the passages.

Paragraph 4:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The notes omit the added reflection and the doubling in the last paragraph, and say nothing about the invented content, so they fail to teach what was changed.

judge.verdict: The rewrite pastes Huck Finn dialect over the passage and adds invented commentary, with some muddled sentences that read as garbled rather than as Twain. The notes cite one line twice with dubious sources and don't report the additions.

Dear Mom and Dad,

Camp is okay I guess. The food is gross and my bunkmate snores like crazy. Yesterday we went canoeing and I flipped the canoe and everybody laughed. It was so embarrassing.

But there's this girl named Kayla who's really cool. She's from Ohio and she knows a ton about horses. We hang out at the lake after dinner and talk about stuff. I think she likes me but I'm not sure.

Can you send more snacks? And my phone charger, which I totally forgot. The counselors are kind of strict but mostly fine.

Love, Jake

P.S. Please don't let Max use my room.
rewrite:
Dear Mother and Father,

Camp is all right, I reckon, though I can't say it any stronger than that. The food is not what you'd call first-rate, and the fellow that sleeps alongside of me snores like he was sawing wood, and never lets up the whole night long. Yesterday the lot of us went out in the canoe, and I tipped it clean over, and every last one of them stood there and laughed fit to kill. It was about as mortifying a thing as ever happened to a boy, I can tell you.

But there is a girl here named Kayla, and she is a right smart girl, and no mistake. She hails from Ohio, and she knows about as much about horses as any man could want to know. We go down to the lake after dinner and set there and talk of this and that till they call us in. I judge she likes me, but I ain't certain, and I would give a heap to know for sure.

Could you send along a few more of them little refreshments, so as a boy has something to eat betwixt meals? And the charger for my telephone, seeing I clean forgot it when I was packing up. The advisers are a trifle strict, but mostly they are all right when you come to know them.

Your loving son, Jake P.S. I wish you would not let Max have the use of my room whilst I am gone.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, “Chapter The Last”, ¶ 13
faults.why: The 'narrator's aside' label is odd for a first-person letter, and the citation is dubious. The notes also leave paragraph 1 with no notes and never mention the "charger for my telephone" change or the added details.

Paragraph 1 (renders the writer’s ¶1):

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.

A new family moved in next door the other day—a father and two little kids—and they come with a wagon so big you couldn't of got it into the barn sideways, which they didn't try, I judge. The dad seems a nice enough man, but the grandmother, she's kind of offish, and a body couldn't say for certain about her till she'd been there a week and showed her quality.

My mother baked them a pan of cakes right off, and she wanted to find out everything about them: where they come from, and what they done for work, and whether they went to church—she wanted the whole of it, and she got it, too, before the cakes was cold.

So then it turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single—well, divorced, which I judge is pretty nigh the same thing after the lawyers get done with it. My mother got a look on her face then, and that look I had seen before; it was the look of a woman that has been trying to set me up for years, and has just found a single man with two young ones and his own ready-made family, and me standing right there with no place to run to.

faults.quote: and has just found a single man with two young ones and his own ready-made family
faults.why: Adds an invented thought to the mother ('ready-made family' and a found single man). It also repeats the 'two kids' fact and goes beyond the writer's 'I knew exactly what she was thinking'.

faults.quote: and me standing right there with no place to run to.
faults.why: Adds a feeling of dread and entrapment that the writer never stated. The writer's tone is wry, not cornered.

faults.quote: and a body couldn't say for certain about her till she'd been there a week and showed her quality.
faults.why: Invents commentary and a judgement about the woman. It softens the writer's flat 'kind of standoffish' into a wait-and-see verdict.

faults.quote: which they didn't try, I judge.
faults.why: Invents an incident about the barn, and the aside doesn't comment on anything the writer said. 'Huge truck' also becomes a wagon, an unflagged anachronism swap.

faults.quote: she wanted the whole of it, and she got it, too, before the cakes was cold.
faults.why: Adds the fact that she succeeded, and how fast. The writer says only that she wanted to find out.

faults.quote: pan of cakes
faults.why: Cookies become cakes. This is a small change of fact.

faults.quote: but the grandmother, she's kind of offish
faults.why: The mend, making the woman a grandmother, is a reasonable repair. But it is a fresh invented person that the rest of the passage never supports, and the family is then described as 'a father and two little kids', which leaves her out. The mend is only half integrated.

faults.quote: you couldn't of got it into the barn sideways
faults.why: The sentence is clumsy and muddled: a wagon in a barn sideways, then a joke about not trying. The follow-on aside reads as a non sequitur.

faults.quote: A new family moved in next door the other day—a father and two little kids—and they come with a wagon
faults.why: It mixes tenses and dialect inconsistently ('moved in' and 'come'), with 'where they come from' beside 'they went to church'. The Huck dialect is patchy and sounds like an imitation.

faults.quote: I judge is pretty nigh the same thing after the lawyers get done with it
faults.why: Huck-style 'I judge' is used three times, including for a lawyer joke that sounds more like Twain the essayist. The narrator's register wobbles between a Huck dialect and a sardonic adult.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 15, ¶ 42
faults.why: The citations are suspiciously exact and probably not verifiable. They are attached to generic moves like 'vernacular voice' and 'deadpan' that don't match the quoted passage, and the same 'which they didn't try, I judge' is listed twice under different chapters.

faults.quote: Sense: Your passage gives the family a mother who is standoffish
faults.why: The notes don't flag the other changes: wagon for truck, cakes for cookies, the invented ending, the 'show her quality' line. They also omit the Pride and Prejudice echo.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the single-versus-mom contradiction and reports it, but it adds invented content (barn joke, 'showed her quality', cornered ending), alters facts (cakes, wagon), and the dialect is uneven. The notes' citations are dubious and incomplete.

The party was at Jessica's house, and her parents were out of town; and everybody from school was there, and the music was going so loud a body couldn't hear himself think.

I stood in the kitchen with my friend Emma, and we didn't know many of the people; but by and by a tall guy came over and commenced talking to us, and his name was Chris, and he was kind of arrogant, only he was funny, too.

He said the party was lame and the people were dull, and Emma rolled her eyes; and I judged he was rude, and the whole shebang had nothing to it.

But along towards the end, when everybody else had cleared out, I seen him helping clean up; and I says to myself, maybe I was wrong about him.

  (no notes)
faults.why: Several moves go unreported there: the semicolon chaining, 'a body couldn't hear himself think', and the dropped 'super'. The paragraph is also heavily changed.

faults.quote: and the music was going so loud a body couldn't hear himself think
faults.why: 'A body' is apt, but the stock phrase is cliché and the added 'hear himself think' is an embellishment. The sentence has no Twainian comic exaggeration or specific detail.

faults.quote: I seen him helping clean up; and I says to myself, maybe I was wrong about him.
faults.why: Mixes Huck-style dialect ('I seen', 'I says') with the otherwise standard narration ('commenced', 'by and by'). Dialect is applied only at the end, and a girl narrator at a modern party in Huck's dialect is incongruous. 'I says to myself' is also an addition.

faults.quote: he was kind of arrogant, only he was funny, too
faults.why: 'Kind of' and 'only' are a clumsy mix. It remains modern prose with 'and' and ';' glue and no real Twain wit.

faults.quote: Everyone from school was there... lame
faults.why: 'Lame' stays modern slang inside a pseudo-19th-century register. It is a jarring anachronism, though it may be kept as the character's quoted word.

faults.quote: But along towards the end, when everybody else had cleared out
faults.why: The original's single paragraph was split into two, which is unnecessary. The 'later' and 'when everyone else left' logic is kept, but the structure was changed for no good reason.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the plot but adds a muddled claim ('the whole shebang had nothing to it'). The voice is thin, mostly 'and... ; and...' chaining plus dialect pasted onto a modern setting. The notes misquote the rewrite and give vague labels with questionable citations.

By and by he moved off and I got the milk, and then I saw my ex up at the counter and I wished I hadn't come, and I turned away a little, but the crowd wouldn't give.

faults.why: Adds invented incidents and feelings: wishing he hadn't come, turning away, the crowd blocking him. The writer said only that he panicked.

faults.quote: and it wasn't the milk that made it so.
faults.why: Adds a new commentary clause that is not in the original. It is more than the voice's gloss on what is there and reads as an invented point.

faults.quote: with the wagon
faults.why: Invents a wagon. The writer said "drove", and a wagon is anachronistic beside telephones and an ex at a checkout.

faults.quote: a guy with a cap pulled down
faults.why: The writer's hoodie became a cap. It is a changed detail, and the notes do not report it.

faults.quote: I saw my ex up at the counter and I wished
faults.why: "Basically panicked" is replaced by a milder, vaguer reaction, so the degree of feeling changes. "Checkout" also becomes "counter".

faults.quote: and she looked me over and said, "long time no see—you look great."
faults.why: Adds a gesture, "looked me over", that the writer did not give. It also merges her two separate lines into one.

faults.quote: talking into his telephone the way a man will talk who has got something the telephone wants to hear about
faults.why: A garbled, riddling simile that does not make sense, and its comic point is muddy.

faults.quote: "Hey," she says, and she looked me over and said
faults.why: Tense shifts from present "says" to past "looked" and "said" in one sentence. Later it shifts again to "I says", which is sloppy dialect.

faults.quote: a guy with a cap pulled down
faults.why: "Guy", "ex", "checkout" and "awkward" are modern words that sit awkwardly against the Huck-like dialect, so the result is a patchwork of voices.

faults.quote: most awkward ten minutes I have put in all this week
faults.why: This is a mix of Huck's dialect with a more polished Twain narrator. "Honest" and "I have put in" are not wholly consistent with it.

faults.quote: “I grabbed up my keys and struck out for the store, and took the wagon, and was there in no flat time.” — cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 18, ¶ 79

faults.quote: “He never so much as looked at me, and went right on talking, and I judged he would have talked till morning if the telephone would have stood it.”
faults.why: The quoted line differs from the rewrite, which has "went right on with his talk" and "the instrument". The notes misreport the text.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has some Huck Finn flavor, but it invents incidents and feelings (wishing he hadn't come, turning away, the crowd, the wagon), and one simile is garbled. Its notes misquote the rewrite and give doubtful citations.

faults.quote: I ain’t for shipping without it.
faults.why: Softens Sam's 'I don't want us shipping without it', which includes the team. The 'for' construction also shifts the tone toward a stance or vote.

faults.quote: Quick word: the launching is moved from Tuesday over to Thursday.
faults.why: This is a mild, generic folksy tweak. 'The launching' is awkward and not distinctively Twain. The mix of 'ain't' with 'Please have your sections of the deck' and 'Thanks, Sam' is inconsistent, like costume dialect on a modern email.

faults.quote: The lawyers ain’t yet set their hand to the pricing page
faults.why: 'Set their hand to' is archaic and legalistic rather than Twain's vernacular. Twain would be more vivid or humorous about lawyers. The word order is stilted, and there is little real Twain wit.

faults.quote: tell me to-day, not tomorrow—for tomorrow’s too late to mend it.
faults.why: 'to-day' is hyphenated while 'tomorrow' is not, which is inconsistent. 'Too late to mend it' has a vague referent. The double 'for' clauses with em-dashes repeat the same structure.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 33, ¶ 53
faults.why: The cited passages do not plausibly exemplify the moves named. A 'vernacular voice' note on a plain statement is vague, and the specific paragraph citations look unreliable or fabricated.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “The lawyers ain’t yet set their hand to the pricing page, and I ain’t for shipping without it.”
faults.why: This is a simple compound sentence, not a cumulative one. The note mislabels it, and the cited source (ch. 1, ¶ 2) does not teach the move.

faults.quote: The narrator’s aside: “If you’re blocked, tell me to-day, not tomorrow—for tomorrow’s too late to mend it.”
faults.why: This is not an aside by a narrator. It is an added justification, and the note does not report that content was added.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon—every last one of them, mind, for a deck with a page missing is no deck at all.”
faults.why: Calling this an 'ironic verdict' is inaccurate, because it is a sincere maxim. The note also does not flag the invented content. Notes are given per paragraph, with empty entries for paragraphs 1 and 4 and no mention of the greeting or sign-off changes.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam
faults.why: The sign-off is collapsed onto one line, losing the original's line break and structure. The 'Hi, team,' comma is also added.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the email's basic facts and structure, but it adds two invented justifications and uses a thin, inconsistent dialect that is not truly Twain. The notes mislabel the moves and the citations look dubious.

Things I did on Saturday: cleaned the gutters, fixed the leaky sink, and called my grandmother, who talked for an hour about her neighbor's cat.

By the evening I was exhausted but weirdly proud of myself.
rewrite: Things I done Saturday: I cleaned out the gutters, and fixed the leaky sink, and called up my grandmother, that talked a solid hour about her neighbor's cat. By evening I was tired out, but very proud of myself.

rows.text: Things I done Saturday: I cleaned out the gutters, and fixed the leaky sink, and called up my grandmother, that talked a solid hour about her neighbor's cat. By evening I was tired out, but very proud of myself.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: Things I done Saturday
that talked a solid hour about her neighbor's cat
I cleaned out the gutters, and fixed the leaky sink, and called up my grandmother
notes.cite: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, ch. 29, ¶ 1

notes.after: but strangely proud of myself

faults.quote: tired out, but very proud of myself
faults.why: The writer said 'exhausted' and 'weirdly proud'. 'Tired out' weakens the exhaustion and 'very' drops the 'weirdly', so the odd, self-surprised quality of the pride is lost.

faults.quote: “but strangely proud of myself” — cites The Innocents Abroad, ch. 67, ¶ 44
faults.why: The note quotes words that are not in the rewrite, which says 'very proud'. It also calls this exaggeration, but nothing is exaggerated. The citation looks invented.

faults.quote: Deadpan: “that talked a solid hour about her neighbor's cat” — cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 33, ¶ 24
faults.why: The note claims a precise source for a move that is a plain restatement. 'A solid hour' keeps the writer's 'an hour' with a mild intensifier. The precise paragraph citations look fabricated and teach little.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “I cleaned out the gutters, and fixed the leaky sink, and called up my grandmother” — cites The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, ch. 29, ¶ 1
faults.why: Polysyndeton is a generic device. Tying it to a specific Tom Sawyer paragraph is dubious, and the note does not explain what it teaches.

faults.quote: Things I done Saturday: I cleaned out the gutters
faults.why: Dialect is applied inconsistently: 'done' is Huck-like, but 'I cleaned', 'called up' and 'tired out' are standard. Huck's vernacular is also not really Twain's own narrative voice. The result is a thin costume with no Twain humor, such as a wry aside, a mock-grave comparison, or a deflating turn on the grandmother or the pride.

faults.quote: By evening I was tired out, but very proud of myself.
faults.why: The sentence is flat modern prose. It has no Twainian commentary or ironic framing, so the rewrite barely shows the writer's passage as Twain would have written it.

faults.quote: called up my grandmother, that talked a solid hour
faults.why: Using 'that' as a relative pronoun for a person is a dialect touch that clashes with the otherwise standard narration. 'Things I done' also sits oddly against 'I cleaned'.

faults.quote: By evening I was tired out
faults.why: The writer's two paragraphs are merged into one, which the note acknowledges. The writer's paragraph break, which set off the closing feeling, is lost for no clear gain.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts but is nearly a straight paraphrase with a few dialect markers. It dilutes 'exhausted' and 'weirdly proud', and adds almost no Twain wit. The notes cite precise sources for moves that are generic or absent from the text, and one quoted phrase ('strangely proud') does not appear in the rewrite.

I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite:
I've only been to Paris once, and that was enough. The whole of that week it rained, and rained hard, as if it meant to wash the town clean and hadn't the strength for it; and my brother, he lost his passport on the second day, and after that we saw the inside of the embassy more than Paris itself.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy, and I judge it was the best part of the trip, for there is one place to sit and nothing to lose, which is more than the streets could say. But my brother, he still says it was the best vacation he ever had, and maybe it was—a rainy week indoors, and a new passport into the bargain.

rows.text: I've only been to Paris once, and that was enough. The whole of that week it rained, and rained hard, as if it meant to wash the town clean and hadn't the strength for it; and my brother, he lost his passport on the second day, and after that we saw the inside of the embassy more than Paris itself.

notes.text: Sentence 2 says the passport was lost on the second day, and sentence 3 says most of the trip was spent at the embassy; the cause of that is the lost passport, so the two facts hang together only if stated in order. I kept the order and joined the two, so the lost passport is plainly what sent them to the embassy for the rest of the week.
notes.after: and my brother, he lost his passport on the second day, and after that we saw the inside of the embassy more than Paris itself.

notes.text: The opening sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris, while sentence 2 says she was there and describes the trip; a reader cannot accept both. I changed the first sentence to say she has been only once, the least change that lets the rainy week, the lost passport and the embassy stand as written, and it matches the rest of the passage, which treats the visit as real.
notes.after: I've only been to Paris once, and that was enough.

notes.after: and I judge it was the best part of the trip, for there is one place to sit and nothing to lose, which is more than the streets could say.

faults.quote: I judge it was the best part of the trip, for there is one place to sit and nothing to lose, which is more than the streets could say.
faults.why: Adds a new claim: the narrator says the embassy was the best part, which the writer never said. It is an invented opinion, not commentary on what is there, and it muddles the brother's 'best vacation' point.

faults.quote: and that was enough.
faults.why: Invents a feeling (the narrator's verdict on Paris) that the draft lacks.

faults.quote: and a new passport into the bargain
faults.why: Invents an incident: the passport being replaced is never stated in the draft.

faults.quote: as if it meant to wash the town clean and hadn't the strength for it
faults.why: Adds a figurative embellishment that is not in the draft. It is voice commentary, but it makes the rain feel less relentless than 'the whole week'.

faults.quote: and after that we saw the inside of the embassy more than Paris itself.
faults.why: Moves the embassy fact into paragraph 1 and then repeats it in paragraph 2 ('We spent most of the trip at the embassy'), restructuring and duplicating the content.

faults.quote: I've only been to Paris once, and that was enough.
faults.why: The contradiction is mended by dropping 'never', which is acceptable, but it discards the possible joke reading (never saw Paris, only the embassy). The mending also contradicts the draft's 'the last time I was there', which implies several visits.

faults.quote: The opening sentence says the narrator has never been to Paris, while sentence 2 says she was there
faults.why: Assumes the narrator is female; nothing in the draft says so. The note also does not mention the added 'that was enough'.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 15, ¶ 34
faults.why: The cited source is dubious and precise paragraph numbers look fabricated. The Pudd'nhead Wilson and Roughing It citations are likewise unlikely to support the claimed moves.

faults.quote: Sentence 2 says the passport was lost on the second day, and sentence 3 says most of the trip was spent at the embassy
faults.why: The sense note claims a repair for something that was not a fault. It also does not report the additions: the 'best part' opinion and the new passport.

faults.quote: and my brother, he lost his passport
faults.why: The doubled subject ('my brother, he') is a crude imitation of dialect. Twain's narrator voice is more often wry and periodic; the phrase reads as a costume, and 'But my brother, he still says' repeats the tic.

faults.quote: there is one place to sit and nothing to lose, which is more than the streets could say.
faults.why: The logic is strained: the streets 'saying' they have nothing to lose is a muddled joke. The sentence reads as a garbled aside.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the contradiction and has a few Twainish touches, but it invents an opinion, a new passport and a 'that was enough' verdict, and it garbles one joke. The notes are weak: the citations look dubious and the added content is not reported.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite: When Dana called our dinner off I wasn't a bit put out about it—not a bit. I was relieved, and that's the plain truth of it; I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I'm not proud of that, neither. I told her it was fine, and we'd make it up some other time. But I don't judge we will.

rows.text: When Dana called our dinner off I wasn't a bit put out about it—not a bit. I was relieved, and that's the plain truth of it; I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I'm not proud of that, neither. I told her it was fine, and we'd make it up some other time. But I don't judge we will.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: When Dana called our dinner off I wasn't a bit put out about it—not a bit.
I was relieved, and that's the plain truth of it;
notes.cite: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 26, ¶ 1

notes.after: I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I'm not proud of that, neither.
But I don't judge we will.
I told her it was fine, and we'd make it up some other time.

faults.quote: I wasn't a bit put out about it—not a bit.
faults.why: The writer's 'wasn't upset at all' is rendered with doubled emphasis. It slightly overstates the denial and adds a protesting tone that was not in the original, though the direction of feeling is kept.

faults.quote: we'd make it up some other time
faults.why: 'Make it up' normally means to compensate or reconcile. The writer meant only 'do it another time', so the sense drifts.

faults.quote: I'm not proud of that, neither.
faults.why: The sense is kept, but 'neither' after a positive clause is a clumsy grafting of dialect. The original had no negative before it for 'neither' to follow.

faults.quote: and that's the plain truth of it;
faults.why: This is a generic folksy filler, not Twain's characteristic wit. The rewrite adds no humor, no exaggeration and no comic comparison. It reads as light dialect dressing on modern prose.

faults.quote: But I don't judge we will.
faults.why: The Huck-style 'I judge' is apt dialect, but the passage mixes Huck's register with a more standard narrator. 'Called our dinner off' and 'put out' are mild and uneven. The 'But' also adds a contrast the original lacked.

faults.quote: I don't judge we will.
faults.why: 'Don't judge' reads ambiguously, as 'don't pass judgment', and so is mildly confusing. Twain usually wrote 'I reckon we won't' or 'I judge we won't'.

faults.quote: I told her it was fine, and we'd make it up some other time. But I don't judge we will.
faults.why: The writer's two paragraphs are merged into one. The note admits the merge, but it removes the beat of the short closing paragraph.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I'm not proud of that, neither.”
faults.why: The label does not fit. This is a plain compound sentence with a dialect tag. The cited source cannot be confirmed as apt.

faults.quote: Vernacular voice: “I told her it was fine, and we'd make it up some other time.”
faults.why: This line is nearly standard English, so it is not a vernacular move. The citation to Huck Finn ch. 15 looks arbitrary. The notes also repeat the same label and give no teaching about what changed from the original.

faults.quote: Deadpan: “When Dana called our dinner off I wasn't a bit put out about it—not a bit.”
faults.why: 'Deadpan' is a poor name for an emphatic, repeated denial. The Connecticut Yankee citation for the 'narrator's aside' is a weak match for a stock phrase.

judge.verdict: The facts and the feeling (relief, dread, doubt) are all kept. The Twain is thin: a few dialect tags on plain prose, with no real wit or cadence. The notes use mislabeled moves and arbitrary-looking citations, and they teach little.
